maintopic: FISHERIES
subtopic: ARRANGEMENT WITH NEWFOUNDLAND TO PERMIT CANADIAN FISHERMEN TO LAND PORTION OP CATCH AND SALT
speechtext:
I wish to make a short statement regarding a privilege that has been granted to Canadian fishermen. Negotiations have been going on for some time between -the Department of External Affairs and the government of Newfoundland with reference to the desirability of permitting Canadian fishing vessels operating on the Grand Banks to land a portion of their catches and salt at Newfoundland ports, following which they would return to the banks for further fishing. They would then pick up their fish and salt before returning to Canada. As the fish gradually pack in the vessel, transferring a portion of the fish catches to shore enables a fuller load to be eventually brought home. The government of Newfoundland has seen fit to grant the request for this year only. The condition attached to their action was that announcement would be made by Newfoundland and
Foreign Exchange Control

Canada simultaneously. It was agreed that the announcement be made at three o'clock to-day.
As a result of negotiations with -the government of Newfoundland, it has complied, for this year only, with a request made to it by the Canadian government. The following conditions are to apply:
1.	The privilege is limited to the calendar year 1944, and is restricted to Newfoundland customs ports of entry.
2.	The master of each vessel is to report to the collector of customs furnishing that olficer with information as to the quantity of salt and fish to be landed together with the location of the premises to be used for storage.
3.	The period of storage is not to exceed six weeks or such period as will allow the vessel to finish its baiting and then return to pick up the landed portion of its cargo for conveyance to a Canadian port.
4.	The owner, or operator, of the vessel makes application to the Newfoundland fisheries board for a licence to import salt, in which will be stated the quantity to be stored and the purpose for which it is to be used.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROL
subtopic: BELAXATION OF RESTRICTIONS ON TRAVEL TO THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I should like to make a statement in connection with the restrictions on pleasure travel under the foreign exchange control regulations. 
The traditional freedom of movement between Canada and the United States has contributed very greatly to the neighbourly feeling and understanding between the two countries, and any interference with this freedom could not be lightly undertaken. It was, therefore, with the greatest reluctance that the government accepted the necessity of imposing the travel restrictions in July, 1940, as a means of conserving Canada's United States dollar resources for essential purposes. It is not possible to make an exact estimate of the amount of United States exchange which has been made available for essential war purchases as a result of the restrictions. The amount has, however, been very substantial and there is no doubt that the restrictions played a vital part in seeing us through a period of critical scarcity of United States funds. Those who have had to forego customary visits to the United States may have the satisfaction of knowing that they thereby played no small part in ensuring that exchange considerations have at no time limited our war effort. I should like to pay a tribute here to the good grace with which the travel restrictions have been accepted by the Canadian people and to the intelligent understanding of their necessity shown by all sections of the American public.
Hon. members will recall that on several occasions since the travel restrictions were imposed, both the Prime Minister and I have stated that they would be relaxed as soon as conditions made such a step feasible. It is not yet possible to remove the restrictions entirely, but I am glad to be able to announce that the government now feels that the foreign exchange position is such as to justify some relaxation. Notwithstanding the difficulties with respect to. transportation, the government attaches such importance to the resumption of normal friendly contacts betwen Canadians and Americans that it has now decided that moderate amounts of United States funds should be made available to residents of Canada for travel for any purpose. It should be clearly understood that the government can give no undertaking that transportation will necessarily be available for all who may wish to take advantage of the exchange relaxation.
Residents desiring to travel to the United States will still be required to obtain foreign exchange control board permits. Such permits will in future be granted, however, in the following circumstances:

United Nations Administration
(a)	Banks will be given authority to sell up to $75 U.S. and approve a travel permit for travel to the United States for any purpose where the applicant has not obtained a travel permit (except for business or in transit travel) within the preceding six months. In order to meet the case of persons who may wish to make only one trip to the United States during the course of a year, the board will approve applications for up to $150 U.S. for a single trip during a twelve-month period.
(b)	Short Form H, which is the common permit used in border communities and which has hitherto authorized the export of $5 Canadian, on condition that the funds may not be spent in the United States except for urban transportation, will be revised to authorize the export of $10, of which not more than $5 may be United States cash acquired as change on previous trips to the United States and the funds exported may be used for any expenditures in the United States connected with the visit there.
The board will, of course, continue to make United States funds available in appropriate amounts where such funds are necessary for travel for business, health or educational reasons.
These relaxations in the foreign exchange control travel restrictions will go into effect as soon as the necessary instructions can be issued by the foreign exchange control board to banks and customs officers. I expect that this will be within the next few days.

speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs):	An
announcement was published yesterday concerning the postponement of the UNRRA council meeting, as follows:
The director general, Herbert H. Lehman, to-day announced that the central committee had decided to postpone the session of the council of UNRRA which had been scheduled to be held in Montreal on June 23. The postponement was made necessary by the emergency restrictions on travel and telegraphic communications from the United Kingdom which would have impeded effective preparation for the scheduled June meeting by European governments.
The central committee of UNRRA decided to meet at regular intervals to consider when circumstances make it possible to set a definite date for the session. It was agreed that forty-five days notice of any date set would be given to the member governments. When a new date is established, it is contemplated that the meeting will be held in Canada.
We hope, of course, that a meeting of the council of UNRRA may be held in Montreal. September has been mentioned as a possible time, but no definite date can be set as yet because no one knows for what period the restrictions referred to in Mr. Lehman's announcement may have to be enforced.

speechtext: Has the attention of the government been called to a decision of His Honour Judge Klein, of Toronto, that order 200 of the wartime prices and trade board superseded municipal building by-laws in Toronto, and will any action be taken to remove this control, to aid housing?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: QUESTIONS
subtopic: WARTIME PRICES AND TRADE BOARD-BUILDING BY-LAWS
speechtext:
Order 200 of the wartime prices and trade board was designed to ensure the maximum use of existing housing in critically congested areas. It permits householders to let or sublet such portions of their homes as they do not require for their own needs, notwithstanding any prohibitory pro-

vision in leases, deeds or municipal by-laws. It does not, however, permit structural alterations that would offend municipal by-laws.
His Honour Judge Klein held that order 200 had the legal force to achieve the purpose for which it is designed. No immediate action is contemplated to remove this control as the order has proved to be a definite aid in making available accommodation that otherwise could not have been offered for rental. Moreover, the order has no apparent effect on new construction.

Is it a fact that the Americans are trying to hire at Vancouver 1,200 men for maintenance work on said highway and 300 men for maintenance work on the oil pipeline from Norman Wells to Whitehorse, Yukon?
The answer, in so far as national selective service is concerned is no. The third question is:

speechtext: Pensions branch - treatment and pension examinations-members and ex-members of the armed forces (present war), $9,000,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to make a few remarks during the general discussion period in connection with a number of matters which come under the pensions department. I hope when the minister replies he will answer the various points that I bring up.
The first point has been raised before in the house. I refer to the insurance principle as applied in the Pension Act. All members are aware that what is known as the insurance principle was inserted in the Pension Act shortly after the last war and remained in effect until some time in May, 1940. At the beginning of the present war the government announced that all benefits of the Pension Act would apply to all soldiers in this war, but, for some reason which to my knowledge has never been disclosed, a change was made by which the insurance principle would not apply to soldiers serving in Canada. It is quite true that some short time ago, after a committee of this house had investigated certain pension matters, an amendment was passed known as subsection 3 of section 11,

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
whereby the pension board could grant pensions on compassionate grounds. I submit that that is not good enough. The type of case that comes under section 11 is the hardship case, and this type of case is dealt with solely at the discretion of the pension commission. I submit to the minister that a young Canadian who enlists in the army, is qualified and ready to proceed overseas and fight, and is regarded by the general public as a soldier likely to proceed overseas, is entitled to the full benefit of the Pension Act, including the insurance principle. As I say these hardship or compassionate cases are only of a temporary nature. They are in the discretion of the pension board and the provision may be cancelled at any time. It seems to me only reasonable that the minister when he makes his reply should give some explanation as to why this change was made in the Pension Act.
I would like to call to the minister's attention a small booklet. There is no date on it, but it was issued, I believe, some time in 1940 or 1941 under the authority of the Canadian pension commission. On page 1 of this booklet there is this significant statement:
The keystone of the pension legislation known as the insurance principle, is contained in sections 11 and 12 of the Pension Act, which in part reads as follows:-
Then it proceeds to quote the sections. On page 3 there is a little insert which reads as follows:
Please insert the following after section 11 (1) on page 3 "Notes on War Pensions."
Note:
In respect of service in Canada after the 21st May, 1940, pension may be awarded only if disability or death is the direct result of the performance of military duties.
I submit that the procedure is hardly consistent with this statement prepared and issued by the board of pension commissioners, that the "keystone of the pension legislation" is "known as the insurance principle." Those are very significant words. It seems to me that our whole pension legislation is built around this one principle.
I understand that a soldier who serves in England or anywhere beyond Canada is covered by all the provisions of the Pension Act, including the insurance principle. But a soldier who enlists for overseas service has nothing to say as to the part of the world in which he is going to serve. He is obliged to go where he is sent, and if his superior officers decide that he is to remain in Canada for service, the soldier can do nothing about it.
While I do not like to cite individual cases, I will refer to one case to show what happened
to a soldier who was injured in Canada and who is not covered by the Pension Act. A young lieutenant went into camp at Connaught Ranges in July, 1943. On the 29th of July, at about seven o'clock in the evening, while he was within the lines of his own regiment, he stepped on a football-he was not playing football-and as a result suffered an injury to his foot and knee. This officer was in the Ottawa Rideau hospital and the Canadian military hospital at Kingston from July 29, 1943, until October 28, 1943. He was unable to return to work until November 8, 1943. He will have a permanent disability, despite all the efforts of the army medical men to assure him that the disability must be from some old injury. During the entire period from July 29, when he suffered the injury, until he returned to work on November 8, 1943, he did not receive any pay or allowances of any kind, nor did he receive any payment of any kind from the army, unless some such payment has been made since May 1, 1944, as to which I have no knowledge. Neither will this officer receive any pension. He is married, and during the fifteen or sixteen weeks he was in military hospital and unable to work, his family had to manage to get along as best they could.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Was he discharged at that time?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
He was in the reserve army and was at camp Connaught Ranges for two weeks. In a case such as this there is no sense of fairness or justice, and the same circumstances can be applied to many other cases in the active army. I think I am correct when I say that other hon. members must have had many of these unfortunate cases brought to their attention.
A soldier on active service in Canada who has the misfortune to suffer some injury while he is not on duty or is on leave is entitled, in my opinion, to come under the insurance principle. A soldier when he is on leave and while he is not on duty is still in the armed forces. He is paid by the army; he wears his uniform; he is subject to military law and military discipline, and can be recalled from leave at any time. More important still, if this soldier had never been in the army he would not have been on leave and would, not have been at that particular place when the accident happened. I have always felt that the army or the pension authorities should assume some responsibility for whatever happens to a soldier while he is serving.
Once a soldier leaves Canada, the department recognizes liability if he is injured while on duty, while he is on leave, and while he is not on duty. In this connection I wish to

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
quote from another little booklet issued by the board of pension commissioners, called "The Duty of a War Pension." This booklet was prepared by John L. Todd, who is described as "lately a member of the Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada." On page 6 of this booklet I read this:
Because it is often impossible to decide whether the disability is due to the risks of a soldier's war service or to the accustomed risks of existence which continue during his service, pensions are usually paid for all disabilities incurred during service.
The difficulty of doing otherwise makes it justifiable to accept all detriments affecting a soldier during his service as being due to war risks and to pay pension in compensation for them.

The booklets are bound in identically the same manner, have the same style of printing, and I received them both at the same time. I trust that when the minister speaks he will explain why this change was made in 1940 and why at the present time the insurance principle cannot be applied.
I would ask the minister also to explain just what happens to a soldier who is wounded and who later receives a pension, is discharged from the army and comes under the control of the minister's department. Naturally, when the soldier is discharged from the army his pay and allowances cease. During the period this soldier is in hospital receiving treatment, and before his case is decided, what is the amount of pay or allowance, or whatever you wish to call it, received by the officer, noncommissioned officer or private? Is this payment less than his former pay and allowances, and if it is, will the minister explain why? Further in the same connection, during the time that a soldier is taking treatment in hospital, is there a deduction of S10 a week or some other sum to cover hospital allowances or treatment? If there is any such deduction, will the minister explain the matter?
Another point which has been discussed every time the subject of pensions is before 
the house is the old question of the onus of proof when a soldier applies for a pension. I cannot understand how the pension board or any branch of the minister's department can evade their liability when a soldier enters the army in an "A" category and is later discharged in a lower category after having service overseas and is held not eligible for a pension. I think the minister will be the first to agree that when a man goes into the armed forces he receives a most rigid and complete examination, together with X-rays and a careful and scientific examination of eye, ear, nose, throat and other parts of the body. If the army is content to accept that man in "A" category, how in the world can the onus of proof be shifted over to the soldier when he is later discharged in a lower category and the pension board rules he is not eligible for pension? When the poor private soldier appears before the pension board he is faced with an array of probably some of the best medical brains in Canada. Why should he have to pit himself against the entire pension board? I know the minister will probably answer, as he did a short time ago in this house, that the soldier is given the benefit of the doubt. I do not think that is satisfactory. The pension board should adopt a very lenient attitude in all such cases, instead of putting the man off by making a decision to the effect that the injury was in the preenlistment period, that it was wilfully concealed on enlistment, or that it was not aggravated by military service.
Up to date there have been a very large number of men discharged from the army-I believe somewhere around 110,000 or 120,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Yet according to a return made last session, the actual number receiving pensions is very small. This is especially true of mental and nervous cases. I for one feel that the pension board has not adopted or maintained a very sympathetic attitude in such cases. It is not fair and just that the soldier who has suffered a head injury overseas should be brushed aside by the board, treated as a "lead-swinger," told that his injury is more or less imaginary, and that the best thing he can do is to forget about it and go back to work.
I should like to outline briefly to the minister one of these very distressing cases. A private soldier of the 48th Highlanders became a dispatch rider while in England. During an air raid his motorcycle crashed and he suffered an injury to his head and one knee. He was kept in hospital for a long period; later he

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
was returned to Canada and discharged in "E" category without a pension. This man was unable to work, because he had dizzy and fainting spells. He was advised to take a vocational course at the collegiate institute in the city of Belleville. He started the course, but after he had had a fainting spell he was advised by the director that it would not be safe for him to continue. This soldier was in "A" category when he enlisted; now, after a long period of service overseas, he is discharged in "E" category without a pension. He had certain qualifications as a stationary engineer, and I would have thought that if he was able to work there would have been a place for him in the army, but the army medical authorities decided that he was not fit to carry on in the army. When he came before the medical authorities of the pension board they were unable to find any disability; in their opinion he was quite able to go to work; he was told to do so, and so far he has received no pension.
I am sure that other hon. members have knowledge of some of these distressing mental cases where soldiers have suffered head injuries. I do not think it is good enough for the pension board to dismiss lightly this type of claim, nor do I believe that that is the kind of treatment which the people of Canada expect discharged veterans to receive. I suggest to the minister that he should have a review made of nervous and mental cases with a view to providing adjustments where no pension has been awarded. It appears to me that in all too many cases the allowances and the pensions awarded by the pension board are not granted to soldiers as a matter of right, as they should be, but are handed out in a very grudging manner; that any concessions which are made by the pensions branch, as announced by the minister from time to time, are made only after long delay, after there have been many debates in this chamber, after the press has taken up the matter, after much pressure from the legion and other organizations interested in the soldier's welfare.
An example of this may be seen in the announcement made by the minister on Monday or Tuesday of this week. These benefits which have been conferred at this late date are at least four years overdue, and they have been pressed for by members of this party and by the legion ever since the war started.

Last year when the minister's estimates under the war appropriation bill were before the house there was a debate on Christie street hospital. Everyone can remember what took place, and the various announcements which were read in the press after the house closed, as to what the future status of Christie street hospital would be. Everyone remembers the many excuses and explanations made by the minister and his department as to why this old boiler-factory of a hospital on Christie street would have to remain, as a hospital for our soldiers. The minister insisted time after time that an extension would be built. I remember one excuse which was given was that because of priorities the necessary material could not be obtained for a new hospital. But finally, at a very late date, the minister had to bow as gracefully as he could to the public clamour of disapproval, and announced that a new hospital would be built north of Toronto, known as Sunnybrook hospital. I hope the minister will give the committee full particulars of what has been done further in the past year. But at the same time I would say to him that he and his department, and those who preceded him, cannot be excused for the long delay in providing fit and proper hospital accommodation for Canadian soldiers. It is quite true that since the debate last year some few changes have been made at Christie street hospital, but no amount of money or changes or improvements will ever make Christie street hospital a fit place for soldiers. It is a disgrace to Canada, and no credit to any government that is satisfied to keep in such a place wounded soldiers from overseas.
As an example, only last week-end I was talking to a graduate nurse who had trained and practised in various hospitals in New York city, many of them in the poorer sections. This nurse had just made a visit to Christie street hospital to see a relative who was seriously ill there.

There are many other objectionable features to this boiler-factory hospital, and I hope that when the minister speaks he will tell us what is being done about the new hospital and how long it will be before Christie Street hospital will be only a horrible memory.
In the matter of the rehabilitation grant, which at the present time is one month's pay and allowances, this amount seems very inadequate. I know-[DOT]

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I should like to draw two
or three matters to the attention of the minister, but before doing so I want to say that I concur fully in at least some of the points made by the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough. The first is in regard to the insurance principle being applied to soldiers serving in Canada. I do not know why it was dropped, and I certainly hope: the minister will give us some explanation in that regard to-day. I believe it should be put back in the act, bceause no doubt injustices are being created in the administration of the Pension Act in Canada as a result of the dropping of this insurance principle.
The second point is in regard to the discharge of men who were admitted to the army in category A-l. Only last week I had
3008	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
the privilege of going through the depot in Toronto and seeing the thorough way in which these men were examined on entering the army. Certainly they are given a good going over; they are examined by specialists of all kinds, and when they are admitted as A-l there is no doubt that they are A-l. I do not understand how these men can be discharged within six months or a year in category E, while our pension department assumes no responsibility for the deterioration which has occurred in their condition. It seems to me that after a man is given a through examination, X-rayed and all the rest of it, and is accepted as A-l, the responsibility for any deterioration in his health rests with the army, because that is where it occurred. The phrase we see on so many discharge papers, "disability aggravated by service but not attributable to service" should be dropped from our vocabulary. When the health of a man has deteriorated to this extent he should be recompensed in some way. I also had an opportunity to note the thorough way in which the men are examined on discharge from the army, and I must say that is something upon which the department must be congratulated. These men are given a most complete examination, which was not the chse after the last war, and the department has something to go on with respect to any claims which may be made later on.
Some time ago I drew to the attention of the government the desirability of establishing convalescent homes for returned men, and I believe some action is being taken in that regard. I have in my hand an article appearing in the Halifax Herald which states that the government is establishing a health centre on the Rideau river near Ottawa to rehabilitate men suffering from nervous and other disabilities. It is stated also that four other centres are likely to be erected, one in Toronto, one in Montreal, one in London and one in Vancouver. I do not know whether these are all the minister has in mind, but I would point out that of the five mentioned, three are in Ontario, one is in Quebec and the other in British Columbia. Apparently western Canada has been forgotten. I suggest that these convalescent homes be established all over the dominion so that the men receiving treatment in them may be at least reasonably close to their relatives and friends, from whom they may receive visits. I am sure that would help in their treatment, and make their surroundings more pleasant. It is all very well to say that the climate in Vancouver is much more agreeable than that of the western provinces, but I do

not think that is the only thing to be taken into consideration in the establishment of convalescent homes.
I should like to mention also the matter of hospitalization. I believe in Canada to-day, not only among civilians but also under the Department of Pensions and National Health, we are very short of hospital beds and hospital accommodation. I know the minister is endeavouring to overcome this difficulty. I believe plans have been made to build in Toronto a new hospital to take care of large numbers who will require hospitalization. In the building of these hospitals there should be a certain amount of decentralization. Plans I have seen would seem to indicate that all the hospital accommodation to be built is to be centred in certain large communities. I believe an additional wing is to be added to the hospital at Regina, and to the one at Saskatoon. The Deer Lodge hospital in Manitoba will be added to, and there is to be a large hospital in Toronto. But if a hospital is built in Toronto to take care of the needs of our soldiers, it will be found that men from northern Ontario, including points such as Port Arthur and Fort William, who require hospitalization, will have to travel a long distance to Toronto to receive the necessary care.
It is proposed in the new medical health bill now before the social security committee that the provinces, upon accepting the bill, will establish medical health clinics at different points. I suggest to the minister that when that is done his department should be prepared to arrange for a certain number of beds for soldiers in those clinics. Surely it would be much better for those men to receive attention nearer their homes than to be sent to the larger centres. In some cases, of course, special treatment that is required, may be available only in the larger cities.
Large numbers of our men who will return will require hospitalization for a number of years. If the accommodation is centralized it will mean that relatives and friends who might wish to visit these patients would have to go to the expense of travelling long distances. The department would do well to give consideration to establishing a certain number of beds in each of the medical health centres which may be set up under the provisions of the legislation now before the special committee.
In this connection I received only recently a communication from a town in northern Saskatchewan. Its geographical location is such that great difficulty is entailed in transferring patients from the area to either Regina

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
or Saskatoon. There is no direct train service, and often it takes pensioners in the area forty-eight hours or longer to reach either Saskatoon or Regina. This town and community of Nipawin propose the building of a forty-bed hospital. It is a new area which was established after the last war. To a large extent it consists of people who returned from that war, many of them pensioners who now require hospital treatment from time to time. The letter states further that in this war there have been over 2,000 enlistments from that community. They propose to build their hospital on one of the finest possible sites, one very similar to that occupied by the sanatorium at Prince Albert. It is to be built in a sixty-five acre park, right on the high banks of the Saskatchewan river. They are asking the department to build an additional twenty-bed wing to take care of the soldiers who will return from this war, and the veterans of the last one. The Department of Pensions and National Health would do well to consider decentralization of hospital facilities, particularly in view of the fact that we shall have to take care of a great many returned men.
Another matter that has been brought to my attention in letters I have received is the question of pre-natal care for soldiers' wives. I have been told that a considerable number of deaths have been caused through lack of proper pre-natal care. It would seem that pensions are not sufficient for this purpose. Of course I know the soldier's wife may apply to the dependents' allowance advisory committee to get additional help in case of necessity. Quite often however in outlying areas these committees are not easily reached. The Department of Pensions and National Health would be well advised to make some regular allowance to soldiers' wives requiring special care at such times.
There are other matters I shall bring to the minister's attention when other items are called.

I would point out that the usefulness or adequacy of the hospital has not been decreasing. If anything it has been getting better rather than worse. I say that because from my own experience-and I know something about the hospital, because it is in my own constituency-I feel justified in saying a word of commendation for the management. Under Doctor McMane, district superintendent, it has been well managed in recent years. While the staff and management have been working under disabilities because of the building itself, its location, and perhaps lack of some equipment-although there is considerable equipment in the hospital-it is my belief that they have done the best they could under the circumstances.
There are two or three points to which I would direct the attention of the committee. In the first instance I believe the time that has been spent on, and the interest shown by members in, the welfare of our fighting forces and the soldiers who will return home, is to the credit of the house. We owe to them a duty, and I am under the impression that in a general way we are discharging that duty to the best of our ability.
About two weeks ago I presented to the house a petition signed by 1,500 or 2,000 persons in my own constituency, asking that the clothing allowance be increased from $65 to $125. That is a petition with which I thoroughly agree. True, it was directed to the Prime Minister rather than to the house and, since it asked for an increase in a money appropriation, technically it could not be received by the house. But in fact it was received and I have no doubt registered in the minds of the government and of hon. members. Although this amount of $65 represents a recent increase, it is still utterly inadequate to cover the cost of clothing required by a soldier on discharge. I have a letter from the Minister of National Defence (Army) to whose attention I brought this matter, which concludes with the following words:

I take it that the matter is being studied by the cabinet, and I hope they will agree with me that this amount should1 be increased. As I say, one must consider increases of this nature when discussing other increases which are, desired. They hang together; they must be considered as a whole rather than in detail. The increase in the allowance granted to a man in order to complete his education on discharge would in some measure relieve the tension caused by the small amount given him as a clothing allowance. I hope that the assurance I have received from the Minister of National Defence that the matter is under discussion will result in a larger clothing allowance to our soldiers on discharge.
It has also been borne in upon me from time to time that a good deal of the objection to the conditions which we have established for the discharge of our fighting men is due to a lack of knowledge as to what actually is being done. I know from my own study of the acts and the various regulations how difficult it must be for the ordinary man in the armed forces or his friends to grasp the details. The literature that has been published is of considerable importance. I have a pamphlet entitled " D Day." The sub-title is, " When the Canadian Fighting Man again becomes a Working 
Man." I wish to commend the people who have produced that pamphlet and1 who I believe are circulating it in large numbers.
More striking than that is a book recently published by a member of the staff of the Department of Pensions and National Health, Mr. C. N. Senior, an executive assistant in the department. The book, just off the press, is entitled, " When the Boys Come Home." He kindly gave me a copy which I read with great interest. The subtitle is, "Their Post-War Opportunities in Canada." This book should be read by every hon. member. It is easy, open reading. I started and finished it in one evening. I found it more interesting than a novel or a stoiy.
It is in story form. I see that one of my hon. friends has a copy in his hand. I hope all hon. members will read it, because it shows a grasp of what the situation really is, to a greater degree than any other document I have read. The author of this book has a philosophy of life and a knowledge of affairs. He went through the last war and has been closely in touch with veterans' affairs for many years. An hon. member calls my attention to the fact that his son is .at present overseas. He has a very personal relationship to the armed forces. He has done his work well, and I understand he did it in his own time, not in the time of the department or of the people of Canada by whom he is paid. I have also been informed that he receives nothing in the way of royalties on the publication, that what accrues in that regard is being given to one of the veterans' organizations or to some fund.

DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to offer a few observations on these estimates for pensions. The previous speaker, the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck), accused my colleague of threshing old straw. Since coming here in 1940 I have found that it is necessary to rehash one's argument, or, as the hon. member terms it, thresh old straw. This is my fifth session, and I have found that a member does not get much for the people he represents if he does not get up and fight for it. My colleague the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough has consistently at all times pleaded for the welfare of all members of the armed forces and their dependents; it is to his credit that he has never missed an opportunity at any time. I should like to congratulate him upon the splendid speech he made this afternoon on their behalf, and I think he is also to be heartily congratulated upon the constructive suggestions he has offered to the minister and his department for the betterment of members of the armed services.
I should like first to make some reference to the insurance principle in pension legislation. The person who volunteers for service in the armed forces must obey orders and serve vrherever he is instructed to go. The insurance principle in pensions, I think we all realize, originated during the last war. It was found necessary to establish that principle in order to prevent certain injustices which prevailed at that time. In 1919, when the Pension Act was enacted, the insurance principle was included in its provisions after due deliberation by this parliament. A few years after the last war, as a result I believe of the urgings of ex-service men's organizations throughout the country, a commission was set up headed by the then Colonel Ralston, now the Minister of National Defence, and acting Prime Minister. That commission sat for a couple of years, and after a great deal of well worth-while work recommended that the insurance principle should be restored and applied to all those who had served. The Pension Act was amended accordingly. At the outbreak of the present war the government pledged itself to apply all the benefits of the existing Pension Act, including the insurance principle, to those enlisting for active service. A special order in council was passed under the War Measures Act giving effect to this pledge. However, on May 21, 1940, the
government changed its policy, repudiated its pledge, and definitely excluded from the benefits of the insurance principle all those whose service was in Canada only.
I have already pointed out that all those who volunteer for active service must go wherever they are directed; they have little choice once they have enlisted. True enough, provision has been made whereby a pension may be granted on compassionate grounds for serious disability or death arising from service in Canada, where those concerned are in necessitous circumstances. I do not think that that should be the law applying to those who have offered their services. But the fact remains that the benefits of the insurance principle have ever since May 21, 1940, been denied to those whose service in the present war has been on active service in Canada only.
In my opinion the pledge given by this government at the start of this war should be lived up to. I think most people believe in that principle, and I trust that the minister will still be able to prevail upon his colleagues to have this provision reinstated.
As to pre-enlistment conditions, I know that the minister has said that the benefit of the doubt should be given the claimant. But in mjr opinion the physical condition of a man or a woman should for all future purposes be considered as that obtaining at the time of acceptance into the armed forces. That unfortunately is not the law of the land at the , present time. In spite of their best efforts, ex-service men and their associations have not been able to secure remedial action in connection with a situation which I have always considered one of the worst blots on pension administration in Canada. Full and generous pension treatment should be the responsibility of the dominion.
In Great Britain the situation is perfectly clear-cut. In the British House of Commons Sir John Anderson recently said:
We establish the presumption that a man's condition as recorded on his admission to the service was in fact his condition at that time, and that any subsequent deterioration in his condition was due to his service.
We provide that there shall be no proof of onus on the claimant, and that the benefit of the doubt shall be given to the claimant.
This is simple justice, and should prevail in Canadian pension administration.
Much has been said on hospitalization. I have pointed out in past debates on pension estimates that all military hospitals should be located in quiet areas throughout the country to avoid undue disturbance of our nerve-shattered ex-service men, and should be surrounded by proper grounds. Too often that is not the case to-day. I am happy to say
3012	COMMON^
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
that in my native province of Manitoba we have a splendid military hospital, admirably located and surrounded by appropriate grounds. Unfortunately that is not true of many other parts of Canada. I am informed that generally speaking the surroundings are very unsatisfactory. My colleague the member for Hastings-Peterborough and others this afternoon have mentioned Christie street hospital in Toronto. I understand that originally it was a factory, which was taken over during the last war as temporary hospital quarters. It is certainly most unsuitable for the purpose for which it is used. On one side are the railway tracks, and the other side, street cars. It is in the midst of a manufacturing centre where there is tremendous noise at almost all times. The surroundings are anything but conducive to the welfare of the patients.
The widow of a soldier who had a pension disability of less than fifty per cent has had something done for her, but I think she is entitled to be granted a pension after the death of her husband, and she should also be entitled to hospitalization and medical care on the same basis as the veteran receiving a war veterans' allowance. We ought to do at least that much for the widows of our ex-service men.
I would ask the minister a question with respect to hospital treatment. The private soldier and other ranks including lieutenant, receive, I understand, the same allowance while they are being given hospital treatment; then the allowance ranges upward for a captain and higher ranks. On what basis is that arrived at?
The clothing allowance has recently been increased to $65, but I maintain when a man who has been in the service for some years and has served overseas is discharged he cannot properly reclothe himself for less than double the amount of $65. The allowance should be further increased.
There are various features of the Sparkman Act in the United States which I hope the minister will consider. It makes provision for certain legal protection for members of the armed services to which I think they are rightly entitled under federal authority.
I realize that some of the improvements which we have advocated in past discussions of the pension estimates have been put into effect; for instance, with respect to the dependents' allowance and the rehabilitation of discharged men. These improvements have been effected following discussions in the house in which members of all groups have repeatedly advocated them. The minister,

being an ex-service man himself, I realize is sympathetic in the administration of his department-very sympathetic. I know that he is eager to see still more improvements made in the treatment of our soldiers and their dependents, and I trust he will be able to persuade his colleagues and be able to bring down measures to alleviate some of the conditions which are not satisfactory at the present time.
I do not wish to take further time at the moment but I shall have questions to ask as the estimates are proceeded with,

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, several
improvements have been made in the treatment of our soldiers and their dependents since the beginning of this parliament. The fight to get justice for them has been going on steadily for the past twenty-five years, and generally speaking quite a bit of progress has been made. On the other hand we did slip and slip badly in the spring of 1940 when we took the insurance principle out of the Pension Act. That was done first of all by order in council, and later the provisions of the order in council where embodied in an amendment to the Pension Act. The minister will remember that there was strong opposition to that proposal in the special committee of this house dealing with pensions; finally, some kind of compromise was reached under which the pension would still be paid, provided the dependent soldier was in necessitous circumstances. I remember that at that time we were promised definitely that a wide interpretation would be given to "necessitous circumstances". I am beginning to believe that that wide interpretation is not being given, or that it is not as wide as it should be. I believe that most- hon. members have on their files cases of soldiers' dependents who have been deprived of pensions as a result of the insurance principle being taken out of the act. I will place on Hansard some figures showing what the result of that action has been in so far as soldiers in this war are concerned. I am dealing now, of course, only with soldiers serving in Canada.
In sessional paper No. 170C, which was tabled in reply to some questions asked by myself, we find this. Eeferring only to deaths among men and women of the armed services who served in Canada, in 458 cases a decision was given'refusing pension. In approximately 398 of these cases it was held that the injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in death was incurred during but did not arise out of nor was directly connected with military service. Then, under section 11, subsection 3 of the Pension Act, 325 were allowed

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
pensions; that is, under the necessitous clause. We find, referring to disability only, that in 28,824 cases decisions were given refusing pension. In approximately 5,843 of those cases it was held that the injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in disability was incurred during but did not arise out of nor was directly connected with military service. Again, we find that under section 11, subsection 3 of the Pension Act, 871 were allowed pensions on account of necessitous circumstances. I should like the minister, when he comes to reply, to tell the committee exactly what that term, "necessitous circumstances", means.
With regard to soldiers' entitlement to free hospitalization, any soldier who is "indigent" can receive free hospitalization, and "indigent" is defined as, "any soldier whose income is less than $1,000 a year." Surely, if an indigent soldier is a man with an income of less than $1,000 a year, then a dependent in necessitous circumstances should be defined as a person whose income is less than $1,000 a year. But apparently that is not the case, because I had my attention drawn to cases where the income of the dependent was considerably less than $1,000 a year and yet a pension was denied to her.

speechtext: Does the hon. member remember what was the percentage of disability in that case?

It was a case of death. The soldier had been killed. The income of the dependent was, T believe, around $600 a year. Although the woman was getting only $50 a month, a pension was denied her. I feel that she should be classed as an indigent so long as her income is less than $1,000 a year; that is, she should be treated in the same way as the soldier in that respect.
There is one other point to which I want to refer, namely the refusal of pension because the disability is of pre-enlistment origin. I can quite appreciate that where disability becomes evident one or two months after enlistment there may be some justification for that stand. But in view of the fact that these men are given a thorough examination -I think the rejections go to prove that- when a man has been in the service for two or three years, undergoing severe training- for example, commando training, which has broken down the health of a lot of men- the government are being very unfair indeed
to the soldier to try to prove that that disability was due to some condition of pre-enlistment origin. I do not think it is altogether creditable to the pensions administration that they adopt the means they do to try to prove it. Apparently a conversation is entered into with the soldier, maybe at the time of the enlistment, maybe at some time before discharge, with a view to getting him to admit that, four or five years or even longer before his enlistment, he had some disability. There is a case on my files of a man who, while working on the railway, had a crowbar dropped on his foot and for three or four months he was disabled; after that he was all right and was able to continue his work on the railway. To-day that man is refused a pension on the ground that the foot disability was due to this accident which happened several years before the war, although he had been working steadily on the railway, prior to enlistment, without any sign of a limp, and several months passed after his enlistment before he had foot trouble, which, he claimed, was due to the commando type of training.
On several occasions the minister has made comparisons between the pensions administration of Canada and of other countries. But if I understand it aright, in England the treatment accorded is quite different. In an issue of the Canadian Veteran dated April 30, 1944, I find this statement :
In Great Britain, for instance, the situation is perfectly clear-cut. One has only to take a declaration made in the House of Commons in London recently by Sir John Anderson. He said: "We established the presumption that a man's condition as recorded on his admission to the service was in fact his condition at the time; and that any subsequent deterioration in his condition was due to his service. We provide that there shall be no proof of onus on the claimant and that the benefit of the doubt shall be given to the claimant."
That is not the law in this country, and that seems to be one main ground of complaint in the army. The two complaints I hear chiefly to-day are: the failure of the government to maintain the insurance principle, and this question of pre-enlistment origin. These are very sore points with the men in the army and the various soldier organizations, and I suggest to the minister that a change in both respects be given serious consideration. If a change is not possible to put the insurance principle back in the act, if the government is not prepared to go that far, the very least it can do is to give a generous interpretation to the clause relating to necessitous circumstances.

Since no doubt we shall have the chance of a thorough discussion of soldiers' affairs when the new department is set up, I shall defer the rest of my remarks until that time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am not going to make a speech, but I have something to say. Any man who represents a constituency which has a voluntary enlistment record second to none in Canada will have a well-beaten trail to the Department of Pensions and National Health. I should like to take this opportunity of paying my tribute to a prince of men, the late chairman of the pension commission, Major General Macdonald.' I found him courteous. I found him thorough. He would obey the law as best he could, but sometimes he had to go beyond. I remember once when I was most urgent in trying to get relief of some kind for a soldier's wife. This particular man had died suddenly. He was a victim of shell shock, and when Major General Macdonald could not find anything in the act to cover this case he secured from some place $25 for me to help the widowed mother and her four boys. Her house had been burned over her head. Three of those boys are now serving in the forces and one is too young. Therefore I pay my tribute to Major General Macdonald, the former chairman of the pension board. I would also pay my tribute to Major General Melville. I had two urgent cases and I did not see any hope for them unless the Pension Act was amended. These two cases have now been handled in such a way that the two boys and their parents are well satisfied.
I' do not know whether the Minister of Pensions and National Health is a believer in predestination-I know his forefathers were- but I know from his conduct that he does not want this country to save taxes at the expense of young men who are risking their lives for the welfare of their country, and who have come back less physically fit than they were before they went away. I should like to know whether it is true that the minister is to act on the theory that we should save taxes at the expense of the returned soldiers. When I think of these young men that I have mentioned, without naming them, I am reminded that they were badly discouraged because one of them had not been in the forces very long. He was more disappointed than anything else because he was not physically fit, owing to a disease that he contracted. He was not able to get overseas and it was the disappointment of his life. I am happy to know that the pension board will compensate him for his risk. I pay tribute to the Minister of Pensions and National Health. I say that it is the duty of every hon. member of this committee to make sure that every returned

man from any theatre of war has his case presented to the Minister of Pensions and National Health. If that is done, judging from my own experience, I am sure that they will be treated in a way which will make us all feel like saying, "Cheerio".

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There can be no doubt that the first concern of this nation is to wage war until Germany and Japan have been utterly crushed. Sometimes, however, I think we are prone to forget that the waging of war is carried on by young men who sacrifice their lives in many cases or their health in other cases and whose dependents in most cases suffer in one way or another; they make sacrifices, some of which are very great. Therefore, complementary to waging war must be care for the men of the forces and their dependents, both while the men are fighting and afterwards.
The statement made by the King's Prime Ministers, published in this morning's papers, contained one significant paragraph with regard to the fighting men. It read as follows:
To all our armed forces who in many lands are preserving our liberty with their lives . . . we express our admiration and gratitude.
That is a noble and proper sentiment at this time, and I hope that the Canadian House of Commons and the Canadian people will always bear in mind those words "admiration" and "gratitude" when they consider the men who have been doing the fighting for them. I think the attitude of the Canadian people at the present time is much like the attitude shown in that statement. People are seeing the wounded come back from Italy; almost every week a train pulls in in some part of Canada with wounded from the front. We are seeing sick Canadians come back in large numbers. It is really amazing how many men have been discharged from our forces as medically unfit. The minister will correct me if I am wrong, but there must be nearly one hundred thousand young Canadians who have been discharged from the forces because they are medically unfit.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Up to March 31 of this year 129,000, I think.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Some of those were not medically unfit.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
