maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
It is going to take a great deal of patience on the part of those of us who have had to remain at home if these young men are to be properly reestablished in civilian life, and a great deal of determination and resolution on our part to see that they do get reestablished. Perhaps it will take a

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
good deal of sacrifice in the way of payment of taxes and in many other ways; but surely the Canadian people will see to it that these young men get a proper start and that those who are disabled are adequately cared for throughout the rest of their lives, and that their dependents are adequately cared for also.
Then there is the attitude of the men themselves to be considered. It seems to me that it is of great importance to have these young men feel that they are being dealt with fairly. If they feel that they are getting a fair chance, that the country is really trying to help them out, I am sure that they will make a great contribution to the life of the nation. But at the present time they are not getting a fair chance in many respects. Take this question of the clothing allowance which has been raised by several hon. members this afternoon and on many other occasions in this house by hon. members of all parties. I do pot think it can be questioned that $65 is insufficient to enable men to get a civilian outfit. The result is that when a soldier is given $65 he walks back into civil life feeling that he has had a raw deal, a shabby deal. He starts his civilian life with that impression, and I think that is very serious. It has a very bad effect on the men who have to go back into civilian life. The same is true of the rehabilitation allowance. I would urge the minister to bring down their gratuity legislation without further delay and provide for a proper rehabilitation allowance for the men who are being discharged. Every day that is lost in bringing down this measure means that perhaps a hundred more men are being discharged feeeling they are not getting a fair rehabilitation grant. That is very bad for the country.
It does seem to me that the government has been very slow in getting rehabilitation plans under way and that there is a tendency to go just far enough to save face, and only to go that far after there has been considerable prodding and coaxing. Now is the time to remedy that whole situation. Now is the time to lay a proper foundation for the care of the men and their dependents.
I was very much impressed by the debate which took place in the British House of Commons last July on the question of pensions for the men who have been disabled in this war. That debate was quite lengthy, and hon. members who are interested will find it in volume 391 of the British Hansard, commencing on page 715. The principal speech was made by Sir John Anderson, the lord president of the council, who was discussing a memorandum that had been brought down
dealing with changes in war pensions. It is called a white paper and is described as command paper No. 6459, dated July, 1943. The British have made changes in their provision for entitlement to pension. A few days ago, in referring to the speech made by my seat-mate, the hon. member for Greenwood, the minister said that the Canadian pension provisions were far ahead of the British provisions, but in at least one respect I think we are behind and should lose no time in catching up. Sir John Anderson explained some of the new features of the British pension law at page 718 of this volume of British Hansard, in these words:
In the redraft we include certain novel features, entirely in the interests o.f the claimants. In the first .place, we establish two presumptions. The first presumption-I am putting this in non-technieal language-is that a man's condition as recorded on his admission to the service was in fact his condition at that time. The second is that any subsequent deterioration in his condition was due to his service.
They also established a benefit of the doubt
provision, so that there were the two changes made in entitlement under the British pension law. Of course Canada has had a benefit of the doubt section for many years, and I am going to read it to hon. members. It is section 62 of the Pension Act:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean that it shall not be necessary 'for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall be entitled to draw and shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences in favour of the applicant.
In effect, that means there is no onus of proof on the claimant, and as far as it goes it is very good. The provision which the British now have in their pension law reads:
In no case shall there be an onus on any claimant under this our warrant to prove the fulfilment of the conditions set out in paragraph (1) and the benefit of any reasonable doubt shall be given to the claimant.
So that these two provisions are practically identical. But we have no provision in the Canadian pension law for presumptions, such as the British introduced last summer. The . wording of the royal warrant with regard to presumptions is as follows:
Where an injury or disease rvhich has led to a member's discharge or death during war service was not noted in a medical report made on that member on the commencement of his war service, a certificate under paragraph (1) -
That means a certificate of entitlement.
-shall be given unless the evidence shows that the conditions set out in that paragraph are not fulfilled.
3016	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
In other words, as Sir John Anderson said, they have now established the two presumptions. They are not absolute presumptions; they can be rebutted by the ministry of pensions, but they have established the two presumptions, that at the time of acceptance the man was fit for the kind of service demanded of a man in that medical category, and second, in the event of his being subsequently discharged on medical grounds, that any deterioration in his health which has taken place is due to his service. I suggest to the committee that our pension law should be' changed to include these presumptions. In this war the men enlisting have had far more thorough examinations than was the case in the last, and there have been many more discharges for medical reasons, particularly for illness, as a result of the health of the men breaking down. Presumptions of this type would1 be particularly helpful in the case of disease. At the present time it is almost impossible for a man who has been discharged through sickness to prove that his disability arose out of or was directly connected with his service. That is the way our pension law reads in the case of service in Canada, that the applicant must prove that the disability arose out of or was directly connected with his service. So that I advocate, and I ask hon. members to consider seriously, the amendment of the Pension Act at this session in order to insert these two presumptions.
The British have made a change also in regard to pensioning men injured as a result of accidents. They have gone quite far, I think much farther than we have gone in Canada. Hon. members will find that dealt with also in this white paper, and I am going to read the provision with respect to accidents:
At present most accidents sustained by members of the forces are regarded as attributable to war service but there are four main categories not so regarded. They are:
, (a) Accidents sustained whilst "walking out" in spare time;-
I presume that would mean a man walking out from his military camp.
(b)	Accidents sustained whilst travelling to and from home on short pass, i.e.. leave of not ni0r? "an forty-eight hours duration (unless the leave is of a compassionate nature);
(c)	Accidents sustained whilst travelling to or from duty when the member has been allowed to live in accommodation privately arranged;
(d)	Accidents sustained whilst actually on leave.
Then the white paper goes on to say:
His Majesty's government 'has decided that under war conditions accidents in categories (a), (b) and (c) can reasonably be regarded as attributable to service. The position of accidents in category (d)-
[Mr. Green. [
That is, while a man is on leave.
-is different. In these eases the compulsions of service play no part and an accident sustained in such circumstances cannot properly be regarded as attributable to service.
Sir John Anderson also dealt with the change in the provisions in the case of accidents. Hon. members will find his explanation at page 722 of the British Hansard, where he said:
We are giving the fullest possible application of the doctrine that a service man places himself wholly and unreservedly at the disposal of the state during his service and we are covering everything with one exception. The one exception not covered is the case of the man who goes on leave, "who is for the time 'being entirely released from his obligation to the state and is just as free as anyone else to do what he likes. If in those circumstances a man in his home falls off a pair of steps while hanging a picture on the wall, and injures himself, he is treated just like a civilian in respect of that injury and not like a soldier.
During the course of the debate one reason given for not covering a man who might fall off a stepladder while hanging a picture was that he would be covered by the social legislation in Britain; of course in Canada that would not be the case; here the poor chap would be just out of luck. However, the British have made this provision for accidents, and I think the time has come when section 11, subsection 2, of the Pension Act should be changed to wipe out any reference to military service in Canada. I realize that it would still be the proper provision for men in the peace-time forces.
At the present time it covers two groups, mea in the war who serve in Canada, and men in the forces in peace time. I think the time has come when there should be a change, and when the provision in section 11 (2), restricting men who are serving in Canada, should be deleted. I do not wish to repeat the arguments offered this afternoon by other hon. members, but I am firmly convinced that the insurance principle should be reestablished for the men in Canada. I advocated that throughout the meetings of the special committee on pensions which sat in 1941 but. unfortunately, at that time I did not receive very much support. The committee found against me. However now there can be no doubt the time has come to make the change. That is the second change which I suggest should be made in the Pension Act at this session.
Just the day before yesterday the minister announced changes in the pension law, changes which we have been urging on the government ever since I came to the house in 1936. We have urged them at every session, but have never been able to get very far. However, I

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
suppose a late repentance is better than none at all, and I am glad these changes have now been made. I shall not go over them in detail, but briefly , they remove the restrictions upon a widow getting a pension, if she was married after January 1, 1930; they enable the payment of an allowance for a wife who was married after May 1, 1933, and for a child, where such child was born after that date.
But the difficulty is this: These changes- and there are others, as well-have been made by order in council, under the War Measures Act. I do not understand why that was done. It seems to me that it should have been done through an amendment to the Pension Act, so that the changes would be permanent. As conditions are at the present time, when the war is over, the War Measures Act will no longer be in operation, and these beneficial changes will expire, unless some special provision is made. I do urge upon the minister that he have the Pension Act amended to provide the presumptions, to restore the insurance principle for men who serve in Canada, and to include the changes which have just been made by order in council.
Then there are two or three other matters which should be dealt with by the government. Take the questions of clothing allowance and rehabilitation allowance. I urge that if these allowances are increased, any increases should be made retroactive. It would not be fair to make the change, say, at the 1st of June, and not have the increased allowance given to the man who was discharged on January 1.
Then when a man is disabled, wounded or becomes ill he is sent to hospital, and the arm}'- gets rid of him just as quickly as possible by turning him over to the Department of Pensions and National Health. I do not think a line should be drawn there. Surely a man should not be discharged from the army, the navy or the air force until his medical rehabilitation is complete, and he is in such condition that he can return to civilian life on pension, if he has not been cured, or can go back to carry on his normal work. The minister may say that that involves difficulties in administration, but I suggest that the approach is wrong. The soldier should be treated as a soldier until he returns to civilian life. Let the army, the air force, the navy and the Department of Pensions and National Health work out among themselves the necessary administrative arrangements. Do not discharge a man from the army to the Department of Pensions and National Health. It would be much fairer if he continued as a soldier, at his regular pay and allowances until returned to civilian life
Then, one final matter I would bring to the attention of the minister has to do with men in the veterans guard. These men are getting old. I do not know what the average age among them would be, but many of them must have reached fifty-five or sixty years. If they have disabilities upon discharge from the veterans guard they would, of course, be entitled to pension. But let us suppose that they are discharged as physically fit-as most of them probably would be. Under those circumstances it will be very difficult for those men to become reestablished at that age, especially if they have been in the veterans guard for two or three years. It would be almost impossible for them to get anything to do when .they leave the army. I do not think it would be fair to force them to accept war veterans' allowances, and it certainly would not be fair to force them to accept relief. I believe that some provision will have to be made for a service pension high enough to permit them to carry on under decent living conditions. This is a question which I think has never before been mentioned in the house, but it is one which must be faced. I do not think members of the veterans guard will be adequately covered by the present provisions for men discharged from the forces.
These are some of the suggestions I place before the minister and the government. I do urge the minister-and perhaps he does not need it as much as some other members of the ministry-that these men of ours must be treated not only fairly but generously. I do not believe that we can possibly repay them and their dependents for the sacrifices which are being made. In my opinion that is the feeling of the Canadian people at large. I repeat, therefore, that they must be treated not only fairly, but also generously.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I agree with those who advocate reinstatement of the insurance principle, and I shall not repeat any of the arguments which have been offered. The minister will recall that on the pensions committee in 1940 I was one of those most vigorously opposed to the removal of the insurance principle.
In our rush to bring in orders in council covering every matter raised in the house, and to try to anticipate the criticisms we may receive in the country, there is the danger of repeating the performance of the twenty odd years between the two wars, when the Department of Pensions and National Health of the federal government was made a very convenient spot at which to dump problems affecting indigents. The result was that in the period between the two wars we paid
3018	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
very little attention to social security matters that are and must be separate and apart from war pensions.
I have listened to the discussion we have had and I have read over the many proposals that have been made by the Department of Pensions and National Health in connection with the whole problem of reconstruction and rehabilitation. I am afraid we are still thinking in those terms. It is my considered opinion that the rehabilitation of the ex-service personnel of this war is closely related to the whole reconstruction problem. I am convinced also that if the national income of Canada is not maintained, if there is not full employment in the country in the aftermath of the war, many of these things enacted by orders in council will not be fulfilled. We must keep our minds geared to the main problem of total reconstruction if results are going to be realistic.
In considering jobs for service personnel when the war is over we must also remember that in this country we have a million and a half workers engaged in war industry. They will also be coming back looking for jobs in peace-time industry. They are definitely a responsibility of ours in the matter of reconstruction. In considering the training and rehabilitation of service personnel following the cessation of hostilities, we shall .have to consider this group in the matter of training and so forth. In considering the whole field of social security problems we shall have to be careful to relate to the Department of Pensions and National Health only those matters that belong to it. I am concerned, as is the hon. member for Vancouver East.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Vancouver South.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Do not get us mixed up.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Yes, Vancouver South; the hon. member for Vancouver East is on his way to Australia.
Very important matters are introduced by way of order in council. Immediately after the war is over, these orders in council will become null and void. Unless the act is amended many of these measures will have no meaning. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South when he says that before the session adjourns the pensions committee should be called together to deal with matters coming within the scope of the Pension Act in order that legislation may be passed to place these within the machinery of pensions and national health so that there may be no doubt about many of the important things now covered by orders in council.
I should like to say something about the administration of the whole programme. It

looks nice on paper and I think it was honestly evolved, but legislation of this kind will be of no value to the country unless the necessary machinery to implement it is placed at the disposal of those who have to do with providing benefits for the service personnel.
I am going to stress something with which I think the minister has had a lot to do but which he may have forgotten at this time. Provision has been made for vocational training of service personnel and the providing of certain rights. When we consider the economy of Canada as a whole, these regulations may be quite fair, but there are sections of the country where they will be of absolutely no value. I wish to refer for a moment to Nova Scotia, a one-industry province and that industry a heavy one. The minister will remember that during the period between the two wars when we tried to give effect to the legislation that then existed we had a certain problem to contend with in the field of employment, vocational training, assessment of pensions and other matters related thereto. A man may return to Ontario and Quebec partly disabled. The medical author-ites determine that he has a ten per cent disability and he is pensioned accordingly. He may be able to go out and find employment and thus augment his pension. But take a man returning to Nova Scotia. His disability is diagnosed by the medical authorities as a ten per cent, fifteen per cent or twenty per cent disability. In effect, in that province he has a 100 per cent disability because he would not be able to take employment in a steel plant or a coal mine. The same thing is happening in this war as happened in the last war.
I appeared before pensions tribunals on many occasions when they came to Nova Scotia to try outstanding cases. They agreed with me and I think they recommended that some administrative latitude should be given the commission with respect to that particular province. In Nova Scotia a man cannot pick up a job as a doorman, an elevator operator or in a beer parlour, because we have nothing of that sort. It is exclusively a heavy industry province. I have had twenty years' experience in trying to make the old pension machinery work in that particular field of employment.
We are up against the same thing in the matter of vocational training. There have been no additions to vocational training facilities in that province since the outbreak of the war with the exception of a small industrial school which was established in New Glasgow and which I believe was supported to some

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
extent by the Clark Ruse aircraft people. Recently this school was closed when the aircraft plant at Dartmouth was closed. Service personnel returning to that province find that they cannot get vocational training in their own province.
There is another handicap which is faced by the service personnel of that part of the country, and which may also be faced by service personnel from other parts. Any man who wants to take vocational training must have passed the eighth grade, and many applications are being rejected on that basis. Vocational training will have to be augmented by providing elementary education to those who are in that position. Otherwise a large percentage of the personnel returning from this war will not be able to take advantage of vocational training. As I say, while this is true of Nova Scotia I assume that it also applies generally across the country. While the regulations may look all right and sound all right from the point of view of the general economy of the country, they are nevertheless very restrictive in that particular area.
Two new departments are being set up. A press release was issued by the wartime information board which led me to believe that the Department of Pensions and National Health was to be abolished completely when the new departments were set up, its functions being taken over by the new departments. The release is headed "Post-wair Planning Information", and on page 6 I find this:
A change in the administration of rehabilitation is also to be made. On April 17, 1944, the Prime Minister introduced in the House of Commons a bill to establish a Department of Veterans' Affairs. The new department will take over all the rehabilitation functions of the Department of Pensions and National Health, and will also take over from the Department of Mines and Resources the administration of the Veterans' Land Act. The other functions of the	Department	of	Pensions	and	National
Health will be taken over >by a new Department of Social Welfare.
The statement	that the other functions of
the	Department	of	Pensions	and	NationalHealth would be taken over by the new Department of Social Welfare led me to believe that it was the intention to fold up the	Department	of	Pensions	and	National
Health as it now stands, and to pass over to the new Department of Social Welfare all problems of service personnel with respect to pensions, hospitalization and so forth.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: All affairs pertaining to ex-service men will be under the Department of Veterans' Affairs.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I am very glad to hear that because I got the impression from this release
that the whole load of social security legislation was going to' be absorbed by the department, which would mean that we would have a repetition of the condition of affairs that we had between the two wars. The release i3 misleading.
With respect to the two new departments that are to be created, I have in my hand a memorandum from the Amalgamated Civil Servants of Canada protesting against the manner in which appointments are to be made. I have no doubt the minister has seen it and I do not want to take up time by reading it. The organization points out, and I think properly so, that we have established in this country the merit system, whereby through the machinery of the civil service commission important positions of the kind to be created in these new departments are to be filled on the merit system. But bill No. 83. to establish a Department of Veterans' Affairs, definitely sets out that the new department may be staffed "notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act".

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It is word for word as it is in the present act and has been since 1928.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Maybe that is why the Civil Service Act is not working so well. I agree with this protest. I believe myself in filling important positions of this kind by examination, and without any regard to patronage, favouritism or anything of that sort. The right man for the job is the man who is qualified for the job, and in setting up the new department the minister should have due regard to that principle.
I am a little bit fearful of this attitude that is developing in Canada that when the war is over everything belongs exclusively to the ex-service men. I think that is the wrong attitude to cultivate because the problems of the ex-service men are definitely wrapped up with the whole future of this dominion. We should have a programme for their complete rehabilitation, with every one of them having the right to work and make his maximum contribution to the welfare of the country'. It is wrong to build up in the minds of the men the idea that when they come back they are to be adopted and given everything in the country, without making any contribution themselves. I think that in setting up the new departments the terms of the Civil Service Act should be adhered to rigidly, including that provision in the act which gives certain preferences to returned service personnel, other things being equal.
I wish to support what the hon. member for Melfort has said with respect to the five new health centres that are to be established
3020	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
in Canada, three of them in Ontario. Of course, there are a lot of votes in Ontario. Another health centre is to be established in Quebec. But the maritime provinces are left completely out of the picture, as are the two central western provinces. I wrote the minister some two months ago that I had seen the announcement of the establishment of these health centres and that none was provided for the maritimes, and the minister wrote me that he would check up on the announcement since it definitely looked like discrimination. Our people in that part of the country are much concerned over it. These health centres are to be, I undferstand, something in the nature of convalescent homes. Well, Mr. Chairman, as you know, we have a large number from the maritimes in this war too; some of them are now fighting in Italy, and some are likely to get hurt and will require hospitalization when they get back. I think it would be a nice thing if we had somewhere in the centre of the maritime provinces one of these convalescent or vocational homes where our people could go and visit those who were obliged to recuperate in these homes during their period of incapacity. I should like the minister to comment on that suggestion when he makes his reply because it does look definitely like discrimination. I can recommend a very nice spot in Nova Scotia for that kind of health centre. It is not in my riding, but it is close to where the hon. member for Colchester-Hants comes from. Some time when the minister gets down to establishing a health centre in the maritimes he might consult the hon. member for Colchester-Hants and myself.
As to the assessment for pensions, I agree with what other hon. members have said. The present system is anything but fair and just. It may be that the machinery, is not adequate or complete. I know the Department of Pensions and National Health is understaffed to handle the problems coming before it to-day, and I appealed to the Minister of National Defence when his estimates were up to allow some of the medical boards that are now around the district depots to help the Department of Pensions and National Health.
I should like to mention, without giving the name or number, one outstanding case. This man served eighteen months overseas. He was invalided home as medically unfit. He had a medical board, which diagnosed his trouble as duodenal ulcer, and the decision of the commission was, "Pre-enlistment condition. Wilfully concealed on enlistment. Aggravated three-fifths in a theatre of actual war overseas. Pensioned accordingly." I cannot understand

how the board could arrive at that decision. If this man had that stomach condition when he enlisted, how could he conceal it, and why should he wish to conceal it? If he had that condition on enlistment, how could he serve with it for eighteen months overseas? The training is hard and tough and the food requires a fairly good stomach to digest it. But after serving for eighteen months overseas this man was invalided back to Canada and the medical board decided that he had concealed the ulcer on enlistment.
That kind of administration of the act in times like these leaves much to be desired. There are a good many decisions of that sort. This definition of disability not attributable to military service is causing a lot of difficulty. A man comes back from overseas, as this man did, with a disability which, it is decided, is not attributable to service; and it seems to me that some men take the attitude that unless a German has sneaked up on you, stuck a bayonet in you and you have a big hole to show for it, your disability is not incurred on service. I hope that as the machinery is developed and the administration becomes more experienced and more men come back from overseas who have actually seen service, there will be a fairer administration of the whole thing.
There is another matter which I bring to the minister's attention because I think it important, although I am not going to labour it. I picked up an article in the Magazine Digest of March, 1944, written by Paul Winterton, Moscow correspondent of the London News Chronicle, setting out the facts concerning a new serum developed by Soviet scientists which, according to the article-perhaps the minister has seen it-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
-is a guaranteed cure for neuritis, arthritis and similar conditions. These disabilities are very prevalent among ex-service and service personnel. In the wet climate of the old country, and particularly as a result of standing in trenches, there is quite a lot of it. I took the trouble to get in touch with the Soviet embassy at Ottawa and to write to their representative in New York, and I have information to the effect that this serum may possibly be made available in Canada. As to the unemployment insurance contribution which is made by the government, we were led to believe that the government paid the total contribution and that when a service man came out of the army, navy or air force, and took employment in an insured industry, he was protected from the day his employment began. The minister will remember that at the last session I brought to his attention several cases which arose in Waterford, Nova Scotia. A number of service men were released to go into the coal mines, but because of a disaster there a number of them were immediately unemployed, and when they applied for unemployment insurance they found they were not eligible because it was required that they should be employed for ninety days in an insurable industry and have made a contribution themselves, or they did not come under the scope of the act. The minister was astonished at these circumstances, as was also the Minister of Labour; they did not know the regulation operated in that way, and both of them stated at that time that they were going to check up on the matter and perhaps have some changes made. I think a change should be made. That was, perhaps, an isolated and outstanding case which might not happen again; nevertheless numbers of men are leaving the army to-day and taking employment. They may work in an aircraft plant, and after a short time there is a lay-off for re-tooling of the industry, with the result that they are out for a month or six weeks looking for a job, and they do not come under the scope of the act. Men are also handicapped by other regulations. They start looking for out-of-work benefits, and we immediately see a runaround which takes months to straighten out. I believe the quickest and fairest way of curing this situation is to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act so that these cases will be within its scope, because if the government is to make a contribution at all it should be 100 per cent. To place men in the position I have referred to is absolutely unfair, and the effects will be even worse when the war is over, because a lot of industry will be on the change and shift. Representation should be made by the pensions department to the authorities responsible for administering unemployment insurance to have this regulation changed so as to protect, from this time on, those coming out of the army.

But I do wish to say something about another feature of this matter. It is disheartening when a young man comes back from overseas incapacitated and after examination is told that he had a pre-enlistment disability which was wilfully concealed. It is hard on these young fellows. We know that probably some of them did their best to conceal some disabilities when they first went overseas. They thought it was their duty and those little disabilities were nothing and would not amount to anything. After all, they had a medical examination and it was up to the medical doctors who examined them at that time to find out what was wrong. I agree with hon. members who have said that when a man enlisted his condition should be assumed to be what was shown on his papers, and not something else. First may I say that the
minister of this department is one of the most likeable of the hon. gentlemen who adorn the treasury benches; I hope he will not put me under the painful necessity of withdrawing that remark. This is said to be the pensions branch of the Department of Pensions and National Health. It should not be so; it should be called "veterans' affairs." We have before us now a bill to divide this department in two, to make twins of it, and this item should be under the pompous name of the new department. In the new order there will be no pensions; there will be veterans' affairs, and these estimates should be designated accordingly.
This item is for an amount of $9,000,000, as compared with $4,225,000 last year. It does not take into consideration pensions paid to veterans of the last war, which should be under this item. There is no possible reason for putting pensions paid to veterans of the first world war among the civilian estimates, while these pensions come under the war appropriation. All military pensions should be considered in the same way; the only difference between the last war and this one is that the veterans of the last war got pensions while the veterans of this war are getting none. They are getting allowances. I denounce most bitterly and with the great-100-190
est vigour the actions of the pensions board who always deny the claims of returned men for pensions. The minister said to me, "We will change the law, if under the law as it stands it is impossible to grant a pension to a man." I say that is not necessary, that we need only apply the law according to its letter and spirit in order that the men may receive the pensions to which they are entitled. During the last war many promises were made by the union government. Men who enlisted were told that they would receive, in the form of pensions, compensation for disabilities suffered during or resulting from their service. The life of a man in the army, the air force or the navy is most exacting. Very often a man is classified, on discharge, as absolutely fit, when actually he is not, when he may have a predisposition to a certain illness or disability resulting from the fact that he has lived a most strenuous life during the years of war. That should be taken into consideration. Many men think they are fit when they leave the army when in fact they are not; it is not until five or ten years after their discharge that they suffer a disabiltiy which perhaps they never would have suffered at all, or would not have suffered until much later, if they had not served in the army. That has to be taken into consideration. It has been my experience that many men who were qualified for pensions never received them because they were told they had applied too late. That is not a good reason.
There is another matter I should like to bring to the kind attention of the minister. Take the case of a young man in the army. He is exposed to cold weather; he contracts a cold which is not properly looked after; it degenerates into bronchitis; his lungs are affected, and he puts in a claim for a pension. The first answer he receives is, "Your illness is not attributable to your military service." Then he is told that he has the right to appeal from this decision, and that he may get in touch with a certain gentleman, a lawyer appointed to look after the interests of the soldiers. He does so, but still he is not successful. There was an orgy of pensions after the, last war, and I wonder why the boards should be so stingy now in allowing pensions to men who deserve them. And, worse than that, it is within my knowledge that men have been told, "Resign from the army, and you will go home." Take the young man who is at camp, under doctors who are not under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Pensions and National Health. Mr. Chairman, I make no apology for speaking at this time upon a matter which is causing such devastation, not only in our armed forces but in the civilian population. I refer to venereal diseases. A few weeks ago two young naval ratings under nineteen years of age complained to me in Toronto that when they were returning to their quarters at the exhibition grounds at night they were accosted by women hanging around the Prince's gate. Only to-day a young airman who had recently spent a couple of days in my home town told me that only three-quarters of an hour after he had reached his hotel room he was called up three times by women whom he did not know to see whether they could come up to his room. This situation is sufficiently serious to justify some consideration at this time. There is a lack of proper control, especially in the larger hotels, over the activities of professionals and, even worse, of amateurs. This has become nothing less than a scandal.
May I refer to an article which appeared in Maclean's magazine of February 15, 1944, written by Mr. Blair Fraser. In it he speaks of venereal disease as saboteur No. 1. Hon. members will remember the illustration that appeared at the top of his article. Among other things, he says:
Lieutenant-Colonel Donald H. Williams, who for the past year has been chief venereal disease control officer for Canada, estimates that possibly 300,000 Canadians have syphilis and that 10 .per cent, or 30,000 of these will die of it.
In the services, of course, the statistics are precise, although the 35,000 total quoted is a computed figure. In spite of numerous requests no recent figures on VD incidence had been published when this article was written.
The figures he gave for the air force show 2-1 new cases per 1,000 per month. In the army there were 4 new cases per 1,000 per month and in the navy 5-29 new cases. Multiplying those monthly rates by twelve we get an incidence per 1,000 of 25-2 in the air force, 48 in the army and 63-4 in the navy. I am 100-1901
glad to be able to say that the army established a department of venereal disease control a little over a year ago and appointed Colonel D. H. Williams as director. He has associated with him liaison officers for the air and navy. His work now extends across Canada. It is interesting to note that Colonel Williams has recently been appointed adviser for the British government on venereal disease control for the Anglo-American Caribbean commission, which will take him to Jamaica and other islands in the Caribbean sea.
The control which the army and air force have now put into effect has resulted in a great reduction ,in the incidence of venereal disease. Our aim now should be the mobilization of the civilian population in a venereal disease control programme. There should be blood tests made in industry as well as beforemarriage. In order to give something of a comprehensive and brief account of the situation with regard to this disease, I am first going to the western coast, to British Columbia, where the first and best work on the control of venereal diseases has been done. I am sure the minister will be interested to know this, although he probably knows it already.
In the Pacific command where a good civilian programme of venereal disease control has been in force over a period of years, the venereal disease rate in the Canadian army forces stationed in that area has since the beginning of the war been consistently in the neighbourhood of one-half of that for the rest of Canada, and one-quarter of what it is in certain sections of the country. In a review of the whole situation certain factors emerge which indicate why British Columbia has led the field in venereal disease control, factors which may serve as a pattern for control in other parts of Canada. Briefly they are as follows:
1.	British Columbia has provided modern facilities for the diagnosis and treatment of venereal disease. The clinics have been made attractive in order to encourage attendance,, and courteous service is rendered at all times. A social service department is maintained, not only to trace contacts but to assist patients in making satisfactory adjustments. A comprehensive record system is another feature,-without which a venereal disease control clinic cannot trace its contacts and cannot measure the success of its efforts.
2.	There is in British Columbia a relatively high standard of living reinforced by progressive social service measures. I wish strongly to emphasize the fact that the fight against venereal disease is a fight against squalor, slums, overcrowding, bad housing, hunger, neglect and insecurity.

3. It is quite clear that the public health authorities in British Columbia recognized that the education of the public was vitally necessary if the programme were to be successful. A separate department was established for the purpose; the hush-hush attitude toward venereal disease was dispelled and the facts were made known. "
4.	With an enlightened public there was community support of the different methods employed to control venereal disease, particularly in regard, to law enforcement. It must be remembered, however, that while venereal disease is a problem of national concern the conditions which facilitate its spread are essentially local, and in the main local action is necessary to meet these conditions. I am informed that the Greater Vancouver Health League, the Vancouver Junior Board of Trade and the Vancouver Council of Social Agencies were and are continuing to be of [DOT]great assistance to venereal disease control .authorities in British Columbia. Might I [DOT] urge that similar voluntary groups throughout [DOT]*Canada be encouraged to participate in a >national programme.
5.	One cannot examine the British Columbia {programme without realizing the importance iof effective law enforcement in controlling venereal disease. In this regard the salient features were as follows. British Columbia did not make the mistake of directing action solely against the prostitutes when tackling the problem of prostitution. It was realized that the girls are simply the employees of unscrupulous third-party interests who are the "facilitators"-those who derive profit from the business but are seldom brought into [DOT]court. Among these are the "madames", the racketeers and the owners and agents of the bawdy houses. If prostitution in Canada is to be brought to a minimum, with a subsequent reduction in venereal disease, the police authorities must concentrate their efforts on bringing these various facilitators to justice.
I next wish to call attention to the necessity of enlightened attitude of magistrates. The futility of imposing small fines for prostitution offences was also realized in British Columbia. Such a practice is no deterrent to a repetition of the offence, and a civic administration simply places itself in the invidious position of deriving revenue from immoral behaviour.

The realistic attitude is to impose gaol sentences for prostitution offences, so that it may be demonstrated that the community will not tolerate the activities of those individuals who are spreading venereal infection.
To amplify this further I would say that a vicious habit has been growing in Canada in cases where prostitutes are brought before the courts, of magistrates giving them a fine, instead of giving a gaol sentence for the third party. The result of this is to force girls back on the street to earn enough to pay the fine, while nothing is done to punish the people who live on them.
In British Columbia it was shown that certain hotels and rooming houses were making their premises available for sexual exposure resulting in venereal infection. It was also demonstrated that infected pick-ups made a practice of congregating at certain beer parlours, restaurants and dance halls. Other similar establishments had no such record against them, so that it was obviously a question of management. Many businesses responded to the appeal of health authorities to clean up, but for those that failed to cooperate' more vigorous measures were necessary.
In British Columbia it was necessary to recommend that the licences of certain business establishments be suspended or cancelled, since they failed to cooperate with the venereal disease control programme.
I should just like to say here that the credit for all this work in British Columbia is due to Colonel Williams, who is now in charge of the national control of venereal disease.
I wrote to a number of the provincial ministers of health and I should like to quote two or three paragraphs from the replies I received from them. First I will read a portion of the reply from Mr. Cross, Minister of Health of Alberta. I wrote him to see what the situation was in his province, as I did to provincial ministers of health in the other provinces. Mr. Cross says:
The grant made last year by the federal government has been of real value to us. It has enabled us to engage additional epidemiological personnel and our staff last year located and brought under control 73 per cent of all alleged sources of infection in this province. This is the top figure for Canada and I believe is unexcelled on the American continent.
It is .possible to control the venereal diseases, but it requires money to pay for the necessary personnel and it requires provincial, local and municipal police forces which can and will eliminate prostitution.
The figures for syphilis in the gaols in Alberta are interesting. An examination for venereal disease, which includes the blood Wassermann test, has been made on every admission to our gaols since January, 1920. For the year 1920

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
the syphilis rate for the gaols was 16 per cent. There has been a steady reduction over the years to a present low of less than 3 per cent. We believe that there has been a corresponding reduction in the population as a whole. The syphilis rate in the gaols is very high because many infected prostitutes are sent there.
From Winnipeg the minister of health of Manitoba writes in part:
Under the present arrangements in Manitoba any individual who cannot afford to pay can receive free treatment for both syphilis and gonorrhoea. In the case of persons residing in the Greater Winnipeg area, such treatment is supplied through a clinic at the St. Boniface General hospital which is subsidized by the department. In the case of persons residing outside of the Greater Winnipeg area we pay the family doctor for treatment given and this under the supervision of our venereal disease control officer.
We believe that all syphilis cases are reported. In Manitoba, all laboratory examinations are done at our own laboratory, and in this way, we have a complete record of positive Wassermanns.
Then he gives details which I do not think I will take time to read.
I have had a reply from Doctor R. P. Vivian, Minister of Health of Ontario, and I wish to read just a few facts which I think are striking:
There have been reported to the department, since the onset of war, more than fifty thousand cases of venereal disease.
In the past seven years, 1937 to 1943 inclusive, a total of almost seventy thousand venereal infections have been reported. More than half of these have been the more serious disease, syphilis, which, if neglected, will continue, in the coming years, to fill hospital beds, mental institutions, and early graves. More important than even this total number of infections is the fact that with every year of the war there has been an increase in the number of oases reported. There were over one thousand more venereal infections reported in Ontario during 1943 than in 1942, making the enormous total of more than 13 thousand in 1943 alone. Some 7 thousand of these were cases of syphilis, and more than half of these were new cases, freshly acquired since the outbreak of war. The most serious fact is that among these 7 thousand people were almost 5 hundred who showed evidence of serious damage to the brain and nervous system.
The importance of this will be recognized when I tell you that, for the past fifteen years, one out of every eighteen persons admitted to our mental hospitals has been a patient until a scarred and riddled brain due to syphilitic infection. But it is not merely adults who have suffered. These figures include a number of tragic cases of little children, born with syphilis, acquired from their infected mothers.
These official figures tell only a small part of the story of this gigantic health problem. From a study of the departmental records, there is ample reason to believe that for every reported case of syphilitic infection there are at least two more people in the Ontario population who have syphilis, wffiich has not been reported, many of whom do not even k now that they are infected. For every reported ease of gonorrhoeal infection, it is believed that as many as four or five other people have this disease.
These cases have not been reported, probably have not been diagnosed, and the treatment has-been neglected.
Hon. members will see at once how very serious it is to have people with that disease going about among the population.
The excessive amount of venereal disease.in Ontario can perhaps be more clearly visualized when I tell you that in Sw-eden, in 1938, the' percentage of syphilis was fourteen persons in. every 100,000 population. In Norway, between the years 1933 and 1939, there were twenty-four people afflicted out of every 100,900. In Ontario, in 1943, there was the staggering total of 175 persons with syphilis per 100,000 population.
That is 12-5 times as many as Sweden and seven times as many as Norway. A new Ontario venereal disease control is being planned with seven important objectives, which I will not take time to give. I should like just to refer to an item published in the Montreal Gazette of February 23 last, which reports as follows:
Blood tests performed on women found in local rooming houses during last week-end's wholesale raids by provincial police resulted in-no less than 33 per cent being declared diseased, it was revealed in police court yesterday.
Of the eighty-four cases for trial, twenty-six: were found suffering from venereal diseases, while twelve of the forty were returned to gaol pending complete cure. Thirty-three per cent showed the blood test for syphilis. That indicates how serious it is to allow these women to be at large. May I express the hope that the provincial police of Ontario as well as the city police of Toronto will follow this splendid example in Quebec and do something about the closing of bawdy houses and dealing more actively with this great menace.
I think I have said enough to indicate the gravity of this disease, so that I will pass on to-something else for a moment. The hon. member for Melfort to-day made reference to the necessity of having convalescent homes throughout Canada, and I want to support his opinion and to say that I think a large number of these convalescent homes should be built. They need not be large, and a number of them could be located in small communities, where the veteran might be near his home. We have an example in Toronto of a charming convalescent home, given by a citizen, Colonel Flanagan, called the Divadale Convalescent home, which was donated to the air force, and where Squadron Leader Doctor Harvey Doney has made a great success of the care of convalescents in the air force.
I do not think it is necessary for me to add anything to what has already been said about Christie street hospital. I am afraid that the minister has become allergic to the name. At

Mr. Chairman, I have listened carefully to the remarks of the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) in regard to venereal diseases. Tha statistics which he has quoted are more or less encouraging for the people and for those who look after their social and moral welfare. This should convince those who believe that the medical profession may still help our people that physicians, whether they be members of the board of the pensions commission or members of the Department of Health, should use utmost care in the examination of men returning to civilian life, whether they were overseas or whether they were simply called up for home defence, if there are still some of the latter. Indeed, soldiers returning to their positions in civilian life should undergo a most thorough examination. There should be no exceptions. Not a single man so unfortunate as to contract what is called for short V.D. should be allowed to return to civilian life before he has been [DOT]cured and before his cure has been definitely ascertained by frequent and thorough examination.
However, if I rise to-night it is not especially to stress this point. I realize that the alarm has reached the whole population through the repeated warnings of the hon. member for Parkdale, who, being a physician, knows what he is talking about in the field of medical science. I wish to deal more particularly with a case which recurs and must doubtless do so [DOT]every time men come back from overseas after having witnessed bombings such as the city of London has undergone in the first years of the war. This man arrives from overseas suffering from a trouble classified as "shellshock". A man enlists voluntarily or is compelled to enlist voluntarily, as you prefer, it all depends on the circumstances. He is sent overseas and becomes a victim of "shellshock"; he was in class "A" or even "B", before leaving the country. He comes back
I Mr. Bruce. 1
suffering from severe nervous shock which practically makes a physical wreck of him. He returns walking with two canes and he may allow himself to be influenced by arguments such as were referred to by the hon. member for Temiscouata, a while ago. Certain medical officers or other army officials will advise him to sign his discharge papers immediately, so as to return more rapidly to his civilian occupation. If he accepts, he is then classified as a case of "preexistent neurosis." Two years ago, when I was in the army, I had a conversation with a prominent army medical man who told me that a ruling had been made whereby shellshock oases would, in this war, be classified as "preexistent". The expression "preexistent neurosis" is a high-sounding one which means that those who return to this country with that complaint will have no chance to obtain a pension.
Some 'cases have been brought to my attention; for instance, a soldier, father of seven children, who had volunteered in the very first year of the war and had spent twelve months in England under the worst bombings. He was serving with an ambulance and each night he had to leave his camp in the ambulance with the medical officers to attend the wounded under a rain of bombs. On his return here twelve months later he was a physical wreck. It was suggested to him, as the hon. member said a few moments ago, that he would stand a better chance of obtaining a pension if he signed at once, and that his case would be looked after more expeditiously. That is just one case, and I know that there are many. There are some which date from the last war and in this war such cases will of course be more numerous. That man had been put in category "A" and his neuropathic history cannot suggest to any army medical officer that his neurotic condition existed prior to his enlistment. I have personal knowledge of that case.
That man who, on his return, could only walk with two canes, spent three months in hospital, applied for examinations, claimed1 a pension, and was referred to various officials. When I interceded on his behalf, I was told that it was a case of "preexistent neurosis". If that man had a neurotic condition prior to his enlistment how is it that the medical officers who examined him, who no doubt asked him questions and put him through a careful examination, put him in category "A". How could he be classed in that category if he was suffering from neurosis? His medical history does not indicate that he ever had any nervous complaint. He had, however, suffered from infection due to the poor condition of his teeth, w'hich had made

War Appropriation-
-Pensions and Health
him nervous for a few weeks but it was not essential neurosis and it could not be preexistent. After that man had withstood bombings during twelve months he was tagged as suffering from preexistent neurosis. If that condition existed prior to his enlistment, how is it that he was put in category "A" and sent overseas? No conscientious physician with a sufficient knowledge of medicine could have put that man in category "A" if he had suffered from neurosis and sent him to withstand bombings. I am not indulging in any bitter criticism, I am simply putting some facts before this house ini order that the minister may take action, if a ruling has been made, without his knowledge, by army medical officers to the effect that a man who returns to this country suffering from a severe nervous breakdown must inevitably be considered as having a preexistent neurotic condition. It is preferable to have at each examination on demobilization a flock of specialists in nervous diseases in order carefully to look into his past life and into his family history, and to ascertain whether the mere burst of a shell may have reawakened a neuropathic condition which could not be detected by three physicians at the time of his enlistment.
Therefore, I ask the department of health, and the minister in particular, to see to it that soldiers placed in category "A", whose medical history does not reveal any serious nervous trouble, but who afterwards become shell shock cases, receive the undivided attention of the medical examiners, and the solicitude of the Department of Pensions and National Health and of the Department of National Defence, and especially the latter, so that these ex-service men, who have done their duty, who have endured their share of sacrifices to defend our liberty, and who have deemed it their duty to volunteer for overseas service, may not find upon their return that the words uttered the other day in England by our Prime Minister were nothing else but words.
The Prime Minister stated, in his speech delivered in England only a few days ago:
We owe it to all who bear the heat of the strife; we owe it to those who are crippled and maimed. . . .
Neurosis is a crippling affection, for even though nervous symptoms are not ever present, the man who suffers from a severe nervous shock, in spite of apparent momentary temporary recovery, is always dangerous. If he works in a factory where accidents are numerous, he becomes a menace to his fellow workers for, on the impact of a sudden emotion or shock he may relapse into this severe neurotic state and provoke accidents among his companions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext: It is incurable?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
I would
not say it is. I know that some cases are incurable, but they are not all incurable.
. . . we owe it to those who are crippled and maimed; we owe it to the many homes that are bereaved; we owe it to the memory of those who give their lives; to do all in our power to ensure that their service and their sacrifice shall not have been in vain.
This man who has enlisted after having been placed in category "A"; who has undergone bombings; who has been exposed to torpedoing in his trips across the ocean; who returns to this country with a promise on the part of the government that his rehabilitation will be taken care of, so he may himself look after his family, knows perfectly well that he will not be in a position to care for his dependents in the same way as before. Although he does not wish for riches, he expects a certain share of the necessities of life. If he suffers from a severe nervous breakdown, with ups and downs, he will not be able to procure the same standards of living for his family. He will be sorely disappointed and cruelly deceived, especially when he is refused a pension.
In the past, the sacrifice of human life in war has been commemorated in monuments of stone or bronze. After this war we must create a more fitting memorial. That, I believe, will -be found only in securing for others the opportunities of a more abundant life.
The returned soldier does not even expect that much; all he wants is to be looked after and decently treated. If, in the past, he has never had any nervous complaints, let us not, after he has been subjected to repeated bombings, tag him as suffering from a neurosis existing before he was placed in category "A" by the army medical officers.

speechtext:
During the last few days a book has been published entitled, "When the Boys Come Home", written by Mr. C. N. Senior, one of the senior departmental officials of the ministry. The first paragraph of the chapter on hospitals and medical care contains the information that when the present war broke out no fewer than 2,300 members of the armed forces of the last war were receiving medical care in departmental hospitals. Many of these, of course, were temporary cases, but a number had been receiving hospital treatment continuously during the intervening years. The salient point about it is that at that time, twenty odd years after the end of hostilities in the last war, no fewer than 2,300 ex-service men were undergoing hospitalization.
3030	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
That gives us a guide to what we may expect in future, and points to the seriousness of the situation we are facing. At the beginning of the war the department had 2,595 beds available ; at the end of December, 1943, some 4,108 had been added, making a total of 6,703. I mention these figures because I consider the accommodation totally inadequate to meet the casualty lists we must expect, unfortunately, in attacking the fortress of Europe. If the raid on Dieppe is any indication at all, the hospitalization already provided by the department is totally inadequate. Please God that Dieppe may not be an indication, but it has happened and we must be prepared for eventualities.
I am not going into the question of Christie street hospital, but anyone familiar with the conditions that have existed for the last twenty years in connection with the care of permanently incapacitated men cannot feel very proud of his Canadian citizenship. On November 11 last I, together with many others, saw the minister turn the first sod at Sunnybrook with his silver shovel. Months later I saw a picture of the area with the rest of the sod still unturned, with the comment that progress at least had been reported because the divot had not been replaced. We in Toronto have a new name for Sunnybrook; we call it "Frozen Brook" now, because we do not know how long it will be until a real start is made on this vitally important hospital. The minister may and no doubt will say that he is being held up because of priorities. Last year I had the good fortune to visit one of the United States bases in the West Indies taken over under lease-lend; to be exact, Bermuda. There they have built not one but two hospitals. The one I saw had completely equipped operating theatres and the very latest medical and therapeutic instruments; a hospital, to judge by its size, with over a thousand beds. In addition, they built for the naval personnel a hospital of something under a thousand beds. So that I say to the minister there is nothing the Americans, at any rate, consider of greater importance than hospitalization, and I submit that there is nothing we in Canada should consider ahead of the hospitalization of those who are risking their lives for us. In the last week or two I had a further opportunity of seeing a large United States service hospital. I think it is invidious that we in Canada should lag, as we do, behind the United States and other parts of the empire in the care and hospitalization of our wounded.
After the war is over we may expect to have a large number of men who will probably require years of hospitalization, and. a few of

whom will require permanent treatment. I suggest to the minister that he establish at once hospitals outside the major cities, away from the turmoil of the great industrial centres, to look after these cases. We have in Canada a large number of health resorts. I have in mind in this connection resorts such as Banff, where tremendous and expensive hotels have been built to care for the tired business man in the summer months. These resort hotels have been well patronized, and I understand the value to those who frequent them is great.
I suggest to the minister that some consideration should be given to the creation of convalescent homes and hospitals in places such as Banff, Radium Hot Springs, Harrison Hot Springs, and all these places are in the Rocky mountains, but there are others elsewhere. At the present time Harrison Hot Springs has been taken over by the Department of National Defence. I suggest that these centres should be used for purposes of convalescence and lengthy hospitalization. We must see to it that the man who comes back from this show is adequately hospitalized.
I can remember when, at the time of the last war, Christie street hospital was opened. Men coming home were placed in old Knox college, a depressing building. They were even put in the cellar of that building-one of the most sinister situations, as anyone who was unfortunate enough to go through that institution will tell.
I shall not take the time of the committee to discuss clothing grants, or other matters at this time. I shall wait until other items of his estimates are before us.
I must say, however, that so far, up to the end of 1943, we have increased our hospitalization by only 4,000 beds-and we are now engaged in the greatest military,-naval and air struggle of all time. If we have the casualties on the scale we have been warned to expect, this accommodation will be hopelessly inadequate. I know there are future plans; but with the progress-or lack of progress-at "Frozen Brook", let me say that it is very little encouragement to the men in the armed forces to see that merely 4,000 beds have so far been provided. And remember this, that at the beginning of this war we had about 2,500 beds, of which 2,300 were occupied.
That is the situation we face in Canada to-day. Nothing could be more serious, and nothing requires more immediate attention than the hospitalization of those who will suffer through actual combat. I say to the minister in all humility: for heaven's sake get on with the completion of, or at least start, Sunnybrook, so that we will know there is to be a real hospital on that site.

When the hon. member for Parkdale took part in the debate he gave some interesting and, I am sure, accurate statistics with respect to venereal disease in Canada, more particularly how it affected the army, and how the disease would be reflected in its effect upon veterans, and the pensions which might be paid to them on account of disabilities arising from such disease.
The hon. member appeared to convey the impression that nothing was being done throughout Canada, and that efforts in that direction were confined entirely to British Columbia. In order to have the record straight let me say that the division of venereal disease control of the Department of Pensions and National Health has already launched a vigorous educational programme for the eradication of these diseases.
The medical profession are glad that Colonel Williams, who is recognized as one of the leading men in the profession in this specialized study, is-now chief of the division of venereal disease control. He is quoted as having said that this easily preventable human tragedy of syphilis and gonorrhoea is largely a heritage of neglect, prudery and failure to face the facts. But it was not until last December, when a national venereal disease control conference was held here in Ottawa, that this problem was really attacked as it should be, and some direction along the lines of an educational and treatment programme was outlined. Up to that time too much attention had been paid in Canada to curing the infection only. The conference which was held was aimed at the sources and causes of the dreaded social diseases, and the deliberations of more than one hundred physicians and visitors from other countries resulted in resolutions which, if carried out, should see venereal disease under control in Canada within the present year.
Perhaps of first importance was the recommendation for a publicity programme to educate the public through the newspapers and by lectures, motion pictures, posters and pamphlets. The venereal disease control division was reorganized last year for an organized attack on venereal diseases, and a consultant in public educational work, Mr. H. C. Rhoades, was appointed to prepare and carry on that programme. At the conference held last December a sort of charter to destroy syphilis and gonorrhoea in Canada was discussed and approved. Social workers and welfare agencies, police and legal machinery, were called upon to aid the physician with his weapons of modern science, while churches and homes lead the fight for better moral fibre in a general dominion wide effort to eradicate 100-191
venereal disease or at least make it extremely rare. The conference drew up an interesting programme. Included in the approved programme were the following points on which the delegates agreed.
First, that they should give the facts. The facts concerning venereal disease will end the conspiracy of silence, banish outworn fallacies and remove false fears. The second point concerned treatment. It was decided that every Canadian who requires examination and treatment should have the best that medical science can provide. Free blood tests, free drugs, free clinics are being provided by the various health departments on the theory that it is cheaper to cure and prevent than to pay taxes to care for the ravages of neglected infection.
Another point in the programme had to do with the abolition of quackery. Laws exist to protect citizens from the quack and the charlatan. Only qualified physicians are permitted by law to care for those suffering from venereal disease. The public must be protected from the incompetent and the rogue. The fourth point in the programme had to do with contacts and the investigation of contacts. Careful search must be made for all who have been contacts. Only by seeking those and by bringing them under treatment and medical supervision can the curse of venereal disease be destroyed.
It is well known that there are different methods of prevention, but the conference stressed two methods. The first was prenatal blood tests. Every expectant mother must have a blood test before the fifth month. They should demand it and insist upon it, because it is the only protection that many unborn children have. In addition to that, the conference suggested and advocated that there should be premarital blood tests and health examinations as safeguards against the sinister encroachment of syphilis upon the home and family.
Because the entire nation is mobilized for war, and because so many thousands are under close supervision in the armed services, Canada was never in a better position to combat the spread of social disease. I again quote Colonel Williams, who said:
To-day as never before, events and conditions are favourable for the final eradication of venereal disease in Canada. There is a full tide of wholesome public interest, concern, and support for measures directed against these master saboteurs of our war effort. Never before has there been such an imposing show of force arrayed against the threat of syphilis and gonorrhoea.
I simply wanted to put on the record what the hon. member for Parkdale could have put
