I do not wish to impute to the hon. member for Parkdale anything which should not be imputed, but I did not hear that particular part of his remarks which would convey the impression that the Department of Pensions and National Health had instituted a programme such as they have. In order that the record might be straight and in order that it might be on the record at the right time, I thought I should say what I have just said with reference to it.
While I am speaking on the war appropriation for the Department of Pensions and National Health 1 should like to make a few observations with reference to hospitalization and the treatment of pensionable war veterans. The present situation with regard to the treatment of pensionable war veterans is that the department maintains hospitals of its own throughout the country or uses facilities of other hospitals in the larger centres. A man who is pensionable and wants treatment must go to these hospitals to be treated by attendants who are employees of the Department of Pensions and National Health. I have heard many complaints about this, from both pensionable veterans and members of the medical profession. Pensionable veterans do not want to leave their own communities where there are proper hospital facilities and adequate medical care to go to centres far distant from their homes. I am sure that this condition could be remedied.
[Mr. McCann. J
As witness of this I would cite to the minister what obtains with reference to the treatment of patients who come under workmen's compensation. I suggest that there are as many workmen compensation cases in Ontario in a year as there are veterans who are receiving pensions who require treatment. Workmen's compensation cases are treated in the hospitals in their own communities by physicians of their own choice. I am sure veterans would be more contented at home and would be able to have some freedom of action in choosing a hospital and the doctor who would attend them. When the war is over, regimentation with reference to veterans should cease. They should not continue to be pushed around as they are when they are told that they must go to a certain hospital.
For instance, take the situation in the Ottawa valley. Any man who is a pensioner and needs treatment is supposed to come to one of the hospitals in Ottawa. Splendid facilities are available in Brockville, Smiths Falls, Perth, Almonte, Renfrew and Pembroke, all wdthin sixty or eighty miles of Ottawa. There are men in those districts equally competent to give treatment to veterans, and I think it is generally recognized that they have as good equipment in those institutions as they have in Ottawa. Furthermore, in almost every one of those communities there are medical men who are veterans of the last war. They feel it keenly that their services are overlooked and that they are not being used for the treatment of their fellow soldiers.
Another matter on which I should like to speak briefly has to do with the remuneration and the salaries of medical men in the Department of Pensions and National Health and' in the service, and the salaries of both medical and dental men who are in the hospital service in the large state-owned institutions. I think they are being grossly underpaid. Men on salary of over $3,000 a year have not received any cost-of-living bonus, and I think it is high time that they received some extra compensation for their services during the war period when they are particularly busy. When we take into consideration the cost of medical education, the long years of preparation, and the comparable salaries which are being paid to men in other professions, the medical doctors in the department of health and the doctors and dentists in our state-owned hospitals who are treating veterans are grossly underpaid. I hope that the minister will give this matter his consideration and see that these men are given better remuneration.
Having brought up on several previous occasions the matter of the use of hospitals

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
in smaller communities and having got nowhere with my recommendations, once again I recommend to the minister that this matter be given his serious consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
There are a number of suggestions that I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I am sure that those who have followed the course of the speeches made to-day have been impressed by the non-partisan attitude displayed by all members to this important problem. As I look back over a period of four years I think of the many suggestions made on the part of His Majesty's opposition with relation to the treatment to be accorded to returned soldiers and other service personnel, and of the number that have been implemented. Year by year we look forward to the discussion of the estimates of the Department of Pensions and National Health, knowing that if our suggestions are able to command sufficient support in public opinion throughout the country they will be finally implemented into legislation.
To-night there are a number of references that I intend to make in as short a time as possible. The first has to do with the estab- ' lishment of the insurance principle in pensions. True enough, in 1941 by legislation the members of this house accepted in principle the order in council that had been passed by the executive in May of 1940. The insurance principle, so far as service personnel serving in Canada only are concerned, was denied by that legislation, and ever since there has been on the part of all soldier organizations and also on the part of members of this house, irrespective of the side on which they sat, a demand that the insurance principle be applied so far as service personnel serving .in Canada only are concerned. There is no opportunity to-day for private members to introduce private bills or resolutions, and I make the appeal to the minister that, without regard to other considerations, he give the members of the house an opportunity at this session to decide whether or not they wish to repeal that section which was enacted in 1941.
I think that if that opportunity were given to members of this house they would, without exception, follow the suggestion that has been so often made by the hon. member for Souris, the hon. member for Hastings-Peter-borough, the hon. member for Vancouver South and the hon. member for York West, that the insurance principle should be applied in so far as those who serve in Canada alone are concerned, to put them on an equality with those who serve elsewhere.
The point I rose to deal with particularly this evening-and I wish to pay my tribute 100-1911
to the courtesy shown by the minister in, allowing me to have a glance at his file in this connection-has to do with reestablishment loans for soldiers and other service personnel, returning from overseas in order to enable them to enter into business and to operate their own private enterprises. To date that opportunity has not been given. There is a suggestion in "Post-war Planning Information", issued by the wartime information board, that one of the subcommittees of the advisory committee on demobilization and reestablishment is considering a proposal that capital advances be made available to exservice men who wish to set themselves up in their own business. This is a very important matter. We are sure, so far as we can be under the legislation that now exists, that discharged members of His Majesty's forces and certain other designated classes of persons will be reinstated in their civil employment under the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act of 1942. Before I pass from that; let me suggest to the minister that that act which we passed in 1942 has so many loopholes in it which only became apparent after the legislation had been passed, that I submit it should be referred to a committee in order to enable the committee to fill in those holes and assure those who serve that when they do come back they will be able to secure their old positions, the ones they left when they entered the armed forces of the country.
So far as the man who desires to go into agriculture is concerned, provision has been made to a greater or less extent; loans are provided for; land can be secured. But for the man who was formerly engaged in business, who had some little business of his own which he gave up in order to enlist in the armed forces of this country, no provision that I know of has yet been made. I speak subject to correction and I hope the minister will correct me if I am wrong.
As I see the position everywhere across this dominion, there are men who gave up their business, small enterprises, larger enterprises in some cases, in order to enlist. I suggest that we are faced with this problem and that we must meet it. After the last war, as of the 21st of November, 1919, provision was made for vocational loans in amounts not exceeding $500 in any individual ease to enable service men to purchase tools and equipment for their reestablishment if they were retrained disabled men, and to pursue their training or education where disability made such training necessary, in cases where they were not entitled to or had not taken training under the Department of Soldier Civil Reestablishment. The record which the minister was kind enough
3034	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
to place before me shows that, of $624,424.48 which was advanced, there was paid in cash up to March 31, 1942, $500,313. In other words, practically all of the advances which were made to enable these men to carry on and to purchase tools and equipment or to pursue training and education were repaid. I suggest that the time has come when provision should be made for loans by the government to men who sold their businesses in order to enlist, as well as to those who have the necessary ability to start small businesses for themselves.
I remember well, a little over a year ago, 'bringing up in the house a case which received considerable publicity across this Country, the *case of a man who had been engaged prior to the war in operating a hardware business. He deft his stock on hand; he closed his business. He was invalided home, and he was unable to get permission from the wartime prices and trade board to enable him to carry on. As the law stands, under order No. 284 no person desiring to establish a business, unless it was operated within a period of one year preceding November 2, 1942, is permitted to do so. In *other words, the men who enlisted in 1939, 1940, or 1941 up until November, who were in business, upon returning from overseas are not permitted under that order to open up the business which they formerly operated, or to start a similar business, without a permit. I believe that certain changes have recently been made in that regard, and those are steps in the right direction. Those changes came about through the fact that matters such as this were brought before parliament. After all, one reason why parliament exists is to *enable those to whom injustice is being done to bring the matter before the house and the *country so that redress may be given. Changes have been made in this regard, and I believe there has been a relaxation of this order, which I will ask the minister to explain, because there is still some doubt as to whether men [DOT]returning from overseas may go into business.
When that difficulty is removed there will still remain another matter, concerning the large body of service people who, having no available funds, and there being no provision for loans to them, cannot open up the business for which they are peculiarly fitted. I do not 'believe there are facilities of this kind in [DOT]Great Britain, but in New Zealand there is a provision for loans of a maximum of $1,800 to *enable a veteran to purchase stock in trade or [DOT]plant or to assist him with working capital. Interest is payable at the rate of four and one-eighth per cent, reducible to two per cent for the first year, or for the first throe years, as the case may be. A similar scheme is in operation in Australia, where advances may

be made by way of loan up to $900 for purchase of plant if the applicant is not eligible under a land settlement scheme. I believe that only in this way, through a government loan or advance to the men who serve, will those desirous of entering into business be enabled to carry on through the difficult days of rehabilitation. I suggest, therefore, that serious consideration be given to the establishment in Canada of a loan scheme such as I have described. We have legislation, introduced at the present session, to enable advances to be made and loans for development work, but as I understand that legislation it will not include within its ambit service men in the position to which I have referred.
Another matter to which I wish to refer is the decentralization of hospitalization so far as out-patient treatment is concerned. In Saskatchewan provision has been made for additional hospital facilities in Saskatoon and Regina, and I wish to draw the minister's attention to the merits of a lake about one hundred miles east of Saskatoon, Manitou lake, near Watrous, Saskatchewan. That lake is known all over western Canada for the medicinal values of its mineral water, the benefits which follow from receiving treatment for those suffering from rheumatism, arthritis and kindred ills. I believe the matter has already been brought to the notice of the minister, and I suggest that consideration be given to the establishment there for outpatients not requiring hospitalization in the ordinary meaning of the term, of a hospital for treatment of diseases such as I have mentioned. This lake has been known for 150 years for the medicinal values of its water.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF PENSIONS AND NATIONAL HEALTH
speechtext:
Which place is that?
Mr. DIEFENBAKER; Manitou lake, near Watrous. The minister knows very well the reputation which the place has. There are readily available facilities. It has the medicinal values, the railway facilities, and an established reputation for treatment; and I suggest that, as far as returning Saskatchewan soldiers are concerned who suffer from the diseases which I have mentioned and related ailments, in order that they may be enabled to receive treatment near home, the necessary hospital facilities might be established there.
One other item to which I would refer is in connection with war veterans' allowances. Throughout this country are a considerable number of imperial veterans who served in South Africa and afterwards came out to this country, who are not in receipt of a pension, having no pensionable disabilities, but who find

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
themselves, with the approach of middle age, the age to which so many of those old soldiers of the last war are approaching, the late sixties, in a position where they cannot carry on. The legislation as it stands to-day denies to them the opportunity to secure the assistance of the war veterans' allowance, because they were not domiciled in Canada at the time of their enlistment, which, as I understand it, is a condition precedent to that allowance being granted. The existence in various parts of this country of old soldiers who have given their best to their country and to this empire, unable to carry on, receiving no allowance, does act in part as a detriment to good morale in the areas in which they live.
The various soldiers' organizations have dealt with this matter from time to time, but as the law now stands these men are denied any such allowance. I suggest that some provision should be made whereby allowances, even on a compassionate basis, should be made available to those old comrades in arms who have served in a common cause with us and within the empire. I think, too, some reciprocal arrangement could be effected between Canada and the United Kingdom or that part of the empire from which those old soldiers came to the end that some allowances may be paid to them. I know of cases in my own province of men who served in South Africa. They are now sixty-five, sixty-eight or seventy years of age. They are unable to work, unable to secure old age pensions, being below the age limit, unable to carry on because no allowances are available. They are dependent on personal support from individuals in their district. I suggest to the minister that an alteration is needed in the regulations as they stand to-day regarding war veterans' allowances, so that those men, in proper cases, may be allowed the benefits of those allowances. That alteration would meet with the support of the members of this committee on all sides.
I think the suggestions that have been made to-day will be most helpful, not only to the minister but to the members of the committee. I know they have been most intensely interesting to myself. In view of the fact that I do not expect to be here to-morrow there is one other suggestion I should make with regard to the question of education of those returning from overseas. Provision has been made in part. I understand the regulations are ready in the United States. I have made considerable study of those regulations. An opportunity is to be given by the government to all veterans desirous of doing so to take college or professional training for one
year after their discharge, with the right, if they have the necessary scholarship and ability, which is to be confirmed or demonstrated by their examination results, to carry on for a second, third, or possibly a fourth year.
The hon. member for Vancouver South said to-day that if there was one thing that should characterize the treatment of the men and women who have served it must be that of generosity. So general' is the desire on the part of the servicemen and women to take advantage of university or professional education that under the present registration one-twelfth of those who are serving in the United States forces have given notice of their intention to take advantage of this further education.

My reason for rising this evening was to place before the minister the claims of imperial veterans who did not see service' with the Canadian army and were not domi^ ciled in Canada at the time of their enlistment ; the matter of decentralization of hospitalization as far as out-patients are concerned, so that they may receive such treatment as near to their homes as possible; and the matter of assuring to those who return and desire to enter into business that they may have an opportunity to do so, which is, denied them to-day, because they will not be-able to. use the ordinary credit facilities which, are available. As the hon. member who has just taken his seat has said, we rejoice in the fact that from time to time we witness improvements made by order in council in the treatment accorded veterans, and that makes it seem worth while for us to fight for still further betterments. If I take a few moments to add my voice with regard to some of the points that have been urged over and over again to-day, it is because with other hon. members on this side of the house I feel that it is worth while to do so. We are glad to recognize that some forward steps are being taken, and we hope that by our continuing to keep these matters to the fore, still further improvements will result. Therefore in just a few words I should like to add my support to three or four arguments that have been advanced quite frequently.
First, I refer to the matter of reinstating the insurance principle as far as men in Canada are concerned. I refer also to the desirability of getting rid, if we possibly can, of the words "pre-enlistment origin" with respect to the physical condition of men who were taken into the forces as A-l. Another point that has been made quite frequently, not only in this *but in other debates, is the desirability of the 'benefit of the doubt, to use the phraseology used by the minister on April 28, really being given to the applicant for pension rights. I know the minister, when he spoke on this matter on April 28, tried to make the point that the law is quite clear that the benefit of the doubt is on the side of the veteran; yet the experience of so many of us in this house is that a great many veterans do not seem to find it that way. It is true that a great many cases we as members of parliament take up with the minister are satisfactorily dealt with, and there is no denying the fact that it gives us a great deal of satisfaction, after taking up a case with the minister, to be able to write back to the veteran who wrote us in the first place and report success as a result of our efforts. But every time we do that we are conscious of the fact that there are many others who perchance have not thought about writing to members of parliament, and still others who have simply accepted the unfavourable decisions that have been given without feeling that anything could be done about the matter. Our attitude is that the situation ought not to be such that cases can be dealt with unfavourably, when upon receiv-

ing special consideration through being brought to the attention of the minister by a member of parliament it can be found that they should have been dealt with favourably in the first instance. I realize that it is difficult to take care of this matter by legislation or even by order in council, but I am satisfied that it can be taken care of, shall I say, by the minister passing the word down through the entire administration of his department that the statement of principle and policy which he enunciated on April 28, and undoubtedly will enunciate again during the course of this debate, is to be carried out not just in theory but in actual practice. I hope we may see a further acceptance of the idea that the onus of proof rests upon the government, and that the benefit of the doubt is really on the side of the veteran.
Another matter that has been mentioned previously to-day is that of more favourable consideration being given to cases of psychological disturbance. We have been quite alarmed by the number of cases of men who are not given favourable consideration because of the nature of the incapacity with which they come back from overseas. I refer particularly to men who have served in the air force. We learn of cases of men whose condition is such that they are no longer of use to the air force, who are discharged after having served for two or three years; yet because the ailment is not strictly a physical one, frequently no pension is available to them. This is a new development brought about by the nature of warfare in which we are engaged during this conflict, and it seems to me that we should find more lenient ways of dealing with cases of this kind.
In thinking about this debate I thought we might not be permitted to discuss such matters as the War Veterans' Allowance Act and the treatment of widows of veterans of the last war, so that it is my intention to have something more to say about those matters when we come to the specific items in the civil estimates. And yet I thought you were quite right, Mr. Chairman, in permitting a discussion at least of a general character on those items during this general debate. Just in passing I should like to say that when we do come to the item having to do with the administration of the War Veterans' Allowance Act many of us will have something to say, because not only are we thinking of the veterans of this war, but we are still conscious of the needs of the veterans of the last war and we want to see them receive the very best that is possible.
When we come to the item in the civil estimates that has to do with the granting of allowances to widows of veterans of the last

war who, when they died, were on fifty per cent pension or less, again we in this group, and hon. members of all groups, will have something to say. We are grateful for the improvements that have been made in these allowances by order in council during the past several months, but there are still some definite improvements that need to be made and, I hope, will be made even before we get to that discussion. I should like to mention particularly the matter of hospitalization for these widows. Further, in connection with hospitalization, I hope one policy which has been in effect will be changed, if it has not been changed already. I refer to the fact that when widows on these allowances are hospitalized a portion of their allowance is paid to the hospital, and another portion is paid to the widow, but a small portion is withheld and not paid to anyone, on the theory that the widow, being in hospital, is getting something extra because of the services provided there. Another matter with respect to these widows comes to my mind because of an order in council which was tabled this week. As I recall it, the order in council provided that the widow of a veteran who was on pension and who, because of the amount of the veteran's pension, would be entitled to a pension herself, now can obtain that pension even though she did not marry the veteran until some time this year. The minister's department is divided into two parts, pensions and national health. I wish to say a few words about the first branch, pensions. The soldiers overseas are very much worried and are wondering why Canada is doing so much for civilians at home, such as unemployment insurance, health insurance and many things like that. Shortly after the war broke out I proposed that a system of life insurance on all our soldiers be established. I proposed it as an economy measure. We all know how complex the Pension Act is, and that it has to be amended almost every session. I have much sympathy with the adminstrators of the act. I have had a great deal to do with the officers in charge of its administration both in the last war and in this war and in the long depression, and I have found that they did excellent work on the whole. True it is that they stick to the letter of the law, and it may be that some of the boards are a little too strict in their interpretations, so that in some cases justice is not done to the soldier.
In the last war Toronto established its own system of life insurance on soldiers who went overseas from that city. We insured each soldier for $1,000, so that he would be free of the worry about what would happen to

his dependents if he should die on the battlefield. Shortly after this war broke out there was an article in Canadian Insurance monthly, describing Toronto's system of life insurance on soldiers in the last war. The United States adopted a national insurance system, and I proposed in this house in 1940 and again in 1941 that we should have a national system of life insurance on all our soldiers, to include provision for their dependents, both during and after the war, and to include, for three years after the war, provision for their insurance against unemployment and want, and free hospitalization.
As I say, the United States adopted a national system of life insurance for their soldiers in the last war, and that effected a very great economy in the administration of relief and pensions. Life insurance to-day is only in its infancy. What the soldier overseas is worried about is this. He goes overseas and he is thinking what is to happen to his wife and children or to his father and mother if he dies on the battlefield. It is a constant source of worry to him. I have received many letters in the last six months urging me to bring this matter again before the house, to substitute in part or in whole for the present pension system a national life insurance scheme paid for by the state. A lady wrote me to-day about it, and I will send her letter over to the minister. She is Mrs. Dobson, a Red Cross worker in a Mus-koka town, and her suggestion is along the lines I proposed to the present Minister of Finance in 1940, that life insurance be provided for all our soldiers. I know a very fine surgeon in Toronto who in 1940 gave up his practice and enlisted. He had a large life insurance policy, but the company changed the policy so that if he were killed in battle his dependents would not collect a cent of life insurance, and the premiums were raised. His dependents would have to depend entirely on the Pension Act.
The lady who wrote me-and she is one of many-points out that we should have a national system of insurance for the dependents at home of those who die on the battlefield. She says:
In many instances young sons, husbands and fathers have carried life insurance in civilian life, but these policies contain clauses which make them invalid in the event of insured being killed on active service.	_
The pensions paid io mothers, widows and orphans are a mere pittance compared with living costs, as also is the cost of living bonus paid to dependents. I am sure you must be aware of the great hardships endured on account of insufficient living allowances. These factors also contribute to juvenile delinquency when a mother is compelled to go out to work to provide for her children.

War Appropriation-Pensions and Health
In the first great war the United States government provided life insurance for her service men and I know it continues this practice during the present conflict. In the former case,
I had a young friend who left ten thousand dollars to his aged father. Part of premium was taken care of by the United States government, the balance paid by the enlisted man. As to this, war, I have a young friend serving in the United States navy who has taken out a policy for six thousand dollars payable to his mother. This too is provided by his government.
I have often wondered why our government has not provided similar protection-surely it cannot be lack of money, when so much is recklessly squandered for far less vital and humane projects.
It seems to me that when a young man gives up the right to protect his loved ones financially, it should be the duty of our government to care for them adequately in the event of his death. From many conversations I am sure that any service man would share fairly with his government the premium on a policy, deductible from his pay as is now done for victory bonds and war savings certificates, which he is expected to buy to help win the war, as well as do the actual fighting.
Unemployment insurance has brought millions of dollars to a fund to protect civilians in case of unemployment. Why not use some of these millions as insurance for our soldiers, sailors and airmen, who have given up the right, temporarily I hope, to contribute to this unemployment insurance fund.
Should consideration not be given to those who are ready to give their all to protect the rights and privileges of us at home, living in comfort and safety? Does an enlisted man not deserve the peace of mind that comes from knowing his loved ones will be looked after adequately?
I want to assure you that my interest in this matter is not of a personal nature. . . .
I know she is a worker for those who have enlisted. She is urging a government-sponsored life insurance scheme for service men, which is what I have been urging for many years. This is a different war from the last, and a changing war. The Minister of Finance has already accepted one proposal that I made to him in 1941 and 1942, for to-day he announced that Canadians crossing the border can now take $150 a year across in United States funds. In view of the magnitude of this, war, I am sure that the more he looks into the proposal I am making that we establish a national system of life insurance for our soldiers, the more likely he is to be in favour of it. I hope that the minister' will look into it.

Mr. Chairman, since this debate has wandered far afield I hope the minister will bear with me for a few minutes while I bring to his attention the fact that a great tragedy befell the people of southern Alberta during the last few months. A preventable disease, typhoid fever, has affected about seventy people in that district. There
was no doubt about the disease being typhoid. Clinical and blood tests established it beyond any question. All of the primary cases had one thing in common, namely, that they had all eaten of some cheese that was made at a special factory between February 5 and February 10. This factory has a good name. It is a cooperative institution. The manager was anxious to do all he could. But it seems that no Cheddar cheese or raw cheese in the whole of the dominion is pasteurized.
It is also a fact that in Canada there have been ten cheese-born epidemics of typhoid, and three of these have been in Alberta. This one was a particularly severe type of typhoid. The patients were very sick; there was about the usual ten per cent mortality; after recovery they will be left in a weakened position, more subject to tuberculosis, and there will be structural changes which will be permanent defects in their tissues. The money cost of this alone to the hospitals and to the patients will run over a million dollars. The long periods of illness have taken people who were needed in war activities, and deaths of people in the prime of life are something to which we cannot attach a value.
Typhoid very often spreads by carriers. There can be the incubation carried, the person who can spread typhoid germs around before he is taken seriously sick; there can be the convalescent carrier, who exudes them for three or four months after recovery; and then the chronic carrier, who for an indefinite period can spread typhoid germs and be a great menace to the district. The provincial health officers after careful and prolonged search, found a typhoid carrier who had been supplying milk to this particular cheese factory, and it was a long search; but undoubtedly the source of the infection came from this cheese.
How can people be protected from such a serious tragedy as an epidemic of this kind is? Inoculations have amply proved their value, but they protect a person only for a year, and they will not protect against massive infection. The pasteurization of cheese is not done in Canada; that is with the raw cheese; it is not processed like packaged cheeses; probably this is not feasible. There is one plan, and that is, by keeping the cheese for sixty or ninety days it becomes absolutely safe; and I want to make an appeal to the minister of health and to his officers to consider making a regulation which will protect people by having the cheese kept for the necessary period of time. If one province only did this they would be at a
Privilege-Mr. Coldwell

commercial disadvantage; but if the whole of Canada did it, the cost would be a small item compared with the costs of such an epidemic.
